Urban data scientist · San Diego

Hi, I’m Johan Fernandez.

My research focuses on GeoAI: what the term means, what separates it from ordinary AI run on map data, and how location-aware AI can shape infrastructure planning and the design of our cities. I use data science, machine learning and spatial analysis to ask who benefits when a model helps decide where public money goes. I believe a city should trust a model’s ranking only when its evidence, and its effect on residents, are clear.

I am currently applying to PhD programs in New York City, where I plan to build GeoAI methods that cities can test, trust and explain. You can read my work so far in my research series, GeoAI for Cities, and in my projects.

GeoAI for Cities · Exploratory research

Manhattan, Measured

A walk through two centuries of spatial research in New York, from the 1811 street grid to FireCast, nearly all of it before anyone called it GeoAI.

Long before the term appeared in 2017, people were using maps, cameras, GPS records and models to decide where New York should build, inspect and protect. Scroll to fly the drone along the route. Each stop is a dated case: what was done, what it found and what it left unresolved. The stops follow the streets, not the calendar; the timeline below the map puts them in order.

Scroll to begin ↓

The stops, in route order

  1. One Police Plaza, 1994: CompStat turned pin maps of subway robberies into weekly mapped crime statistics.
  2. Houston Street, 1811: the Commissioners’ Plan laid 12 avenues and 155 streets over the island.
  3. Flatiron Building, 2013–2014: Place Pulse and Streetscore learned perceived safety from street images.
  4. Empire State Building, 2011: risk scoring raised the share of inspections ending in a vacate order from 13% to 70%.
  5. Times Square, 2009: taxi GPS showed northbound trips 17% faster and motorist injuries down 63% after the Broadway plazas.
  6. Bryant Park, 1968: the RAND fire models, and the fires of the 1970s.
  7. Grand Central Terminal, 2013: FireCast scores about 350,000 buildings for fire risk.
  8. Seagram Building plaza, 1969–1980: William H. Whyte filmed plazas and counted how people used them.
  9. Central Park, 2010: the Green Infrastructure Plan set targets to cut sewer overflows by more than 12 billion gallons a year.

Timeline

Ten cases across two centuries. Read down the last column and a pattern appears: the questions GeoAI now automates were asked long before the methods existed to answer them at scale.

Case studies

Each case in more detail, with what is and is not known.

1811 · Houston Street

The grid as the city’s first spatial model

What happened
A state commission of Gouverneur Morris, John Rutherfurd and Simeon De Witt adopted a plan of 12 avenues, 100 feet wide, and 155 cross streets, creating about 2,000 long, narrow blocks. John Randel Jr. surveyed it.1
Reasoning
The commissioners chose right angles because “straight-sided and right-angled houses are the most cheap to build and the most convenient to live in.”
Why it matters now
Every New York dataset, from tax lots to sensor feeds, is shaped by this grid. A spatial model of Manhattan is partly a model of an 1811 decision.

1968 onward · Citywide (Bryant Park stop)

The RAND fire models

What happened
In 1968 New York began working with the RAND Corporation on computer modeling of city services, starting with the Fire Department. Over the next decade the models informed the closing and relocation of fire companies.2
What it found
Journalist Joe Flood argues the cuts withdrew protection from the poorest neighborhoods, including the Bronx, Harlem, the Lower East Side and parts of Brooklyn, as fires surged. In his account the fires of the 1970s displaced more than 600,000 people.2
Limits of the evidence
This is a journalist’s reconstruction, not a controlled study; other causes of the fires are debated.
Lesson for GeoAI
A model that allocates protection is making a distributional choice. Accuracy on average says nothing about who bears the error.

1969–1980 · Seagram Building plaza

Counting people on film

What happened
William H. Whyte’s Street Life Project, begun in 1969 for the City Planning Commission, filmed plazas with time-lapse cameras and counted how people used them.3,4
What it found
Use depended on simple, measurable features: places to sit above all, then sun, trees, water and food. The city’s plaza rules came to require seating, including one linear foot for every 30 square feet of plaza.4
Published as
The book and film The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces (1980).
Lesson for GeoAI
Detecting and counting people in public space is now a standard computer-vision task. Whyte shows the question comes first: what to count, and why.

1994 · One Police Plaza

CompStat: crime on the map

What happened
Jack Maple, then with the Transit Police, tracked subway robberies with pins on wall maps he called the “Charts of the Future.” As an NYPD deputy commissioner from 1994 he built CompStat, weekly meetings around mapped crime statistics.5
What followed
Versions of CompStat spread to most large U.S. police departments.
Open question
Mapped incidents reflect both where events happen and where they are reported and recorded. The same tension runs through every model trained on complaints or 311 calls.

2009 · Times Square

Green Light for Midtown: taxi GPS as evidence

What happened
The city closed parts of Broadway to cars around Times Square as a pilot, in place from late May to mid-August 2009.6
Data and method
The Department of Transportation compared fall 2008 and fall 2009 travel times using GPS records from about 1.13 million taxi trips in West Midtown and 890,000 in East Midtown.6
What it found
Northbound trips in West Midtown were 17% faster, while southbound trips were 2% slower. Injuries to motorists and passengers fell 63%, pedestrian injuries 35%, and 80% fewer pedestrians walked in the roadway in Times Square. The changes were made permanent.6
Lesson for GeoAI
Location data a city already collects for other reasons can evaluate an investment after the fact.

2010 · Central Park

Green infrastructure by the numbers

What happened
In September 2010 New York released its Green Infrastructure Plan. About two-thirds of the city’s sewered area is served by combined sewers, which overflow into waterways in heavy rain.7
Targets
Capture the first inch of rain on 10% of impervious surfaces in combined-sewer areas, cutting overflows by more than 12 billion gallons a year by 2030, a 40% reduction, for $5.3 billion against $6.8 billion for an all-grey plan.7
Lesson for GeoAI
A citywide target has to become a list of specific sites. Which blocks come first is exactly the ranking question this series studies.

2011 · Citywide (Empire State Building stop)

Scoring buildings for hidden risk

What happened
After fires in illegally converted buildings in 2011 injured and killed firefighters, the Mayor’s Office of Policy and Strategic Planning analytics team, led by Michael Flowers, studied which complaints led to vacate orders.8
Data and method
It combined building violations, foreclosures, tax liens, 311 complaints, building age and neighborhood conditions to rank incoming complaints.8
What it found
Inspectors had found conditions bad enough to vacate a building 13% of the time; with the ranking, they found them 70% of the time.8
Limits of the evidence
The figures come from press accounts of the city’s own results, not an independent evaluation.

2013 · Citywide (Grand Central stop)

FireCast: predictive inspection

What happened
The FDNY introduced risk-based inspection, with FireCast scoring about 350,000 buildings so inspectors visit the riskiest first.9,10
Data and method
Building-level risk scores drawn from multiple city agency data streams; a later version planned some 7,500 factors from 17 streams.9
Lesson for GeoAI
The same city that learned from the RAND years built a far richer model. Whether it is audited for who it protects is the question RAND leaves behind.

2013–2014 · Flatiron Building

Reading streets from images

What happened
MIT’s Place Pulse asked volunteers to compare pairs of street images from New York, Boston and two Austrian cities.11 Streetscore then trained a model on the judgments of more than 7,000 participants and scored about one million Street View images across 21 U.S. cities.12
What it shows
How people perceive a street, safe or unsafe, can be learned from photographs and mapped block by block.
Open question
Whose perception is being learned? Ratings from one group of volunteers may not match how residents see their own blocks.

2014 · Times Square

One hundred fifty million taxi trips

What happened
Researchers built “shareability networks” from more than 150 million New York taxi trips taken in 2011.13
What it found
With modest extra travel time for passengers, total trip length could be cut by 40% or more.13
Lesson for GeoAI
Open city data turned a policy idea into a measurable, mapped estimate, years before the term GeoAI.

Table 2. Then and now: how methods from the walk map onto GeoAI today.

ThenWhat people didWhat GeoAI does now
Street Life Project, 1969–1980Filmed plazas and counted people by handComputer vision detects and counts people and objects in street imagery
CompStat, 1994Pinned incidents on maps and looked for clustersSpatial statistics and models find hot spots and forecast where they will form
RAND fire models, 1968Modeled fire response to allocate companiesOptimization and risk models allocate inspections and crews
Green Light for Midtown, 2009Compared taxi GPS travel times before and afterTrajectory analysis evaluates projects from mobility data
Illegal conversions, 2011Combined agency records to rank complaintsMachine learning ranks buildings, pipes and parcels by risk
Place Pulse and Streetscore, 2013–2014Crowdsourced ratings, then a trained image modelDeep learning on street and satellite imagery measures places at scale
Green Infrastructure Plan, 2010Set citywide targets for runoff captureSpatial models rank candidate sites by value and need

Open questions

This walk is exploratory. It raises questions rather than settling them.

  • Where the data come from. CompStat, 311 and the 2011 complaint ranking all start from reports. When does mapped data show where problems are, and when does it show where people looked?
  • Who audits allocation. RAND and FireCast both decide where protection goes. What would a fair audit of a spatial ranking look like?
  • Whose perception. Place Pulse learned how volunteers saw streets. Would residents rank their own blocks the same way?
  • Evaluation after the fact. Taxi GPS evaluated Times Square. Which other passive data could test whether a city investment delivered?
  • Value and need. Green infrastructure can be ranked by gallons captured per dollar, or by benefit to the blocks that flood most. Which should come first, and who decides?

About

Urban data science and GeoAI, based in San Diego

My research is about who gets what in cities.

When a city can only plant trees, fix streets or fund drainage projects in a few places each year, someone has to decide which neighborhoods go first. I want to know how those rankings get built, whether the data behind them holds up, and who keeps ending up at the bottom of the list.

Where the question came from

On stormwater programs for four cities, I kept the geodatabases that ranked Capital Improvement Plan sites. A fixed set of weights decided which projects moved first.

At the American Academy of Pediatrics I joined Census data to infrastructure layers and kept finding the same neighborhoods short on services.

At UC San Diego I studied Logan Heights and City Heights, where decisions about freeways and housing were often made without much input from the people who live there.

What I'm testing now

GeoAI, meaning machine learning that pays attention to location, could make those rankings fairer, or it could just make them faster and harder to question. My projects test that with public data:

  • Will It Get Built?Which San Diego housing sites are likely to see homes
  • CurbCallHow residents might rank street repairs themselves

That's the work I want to keep doing in graduate school in New York.

Community and equity research · 2023 · UC San Diego

Greater Logan Heights: Housing and Transportation

A census-tract study of how decades of disinvestment in housing and transportation shaped access to jobs, services and opportunity in one of San Diego's oldest Latino neighborhoods.

Seven in ten homes rented, year after year

Greater Logan Heights sits in Southeastern San Diego, boxed in by Interstates 5, 15 and 94. In this part of the city, infrastructure decisions have long been made over residents' heads. In April 1970, residents of Barrio Logan occupied land under the Coronado Bridge after learning the city planned a Highway Patrol station there. They won a park instead: Chicano Park.

The census shows what persistence looks like. In the 2017-2021 data, 70.9% of occupied units in Greater Logan Heights were rented, against about 53% citywide. That share has held near 70% since 2005-2009. Over the same years, more workers drove to work, while transit, walking and biking declined.

Working with the Logan Heights Community Development Corporation, we asked how changes in housing and transportation have shaped residents' access to jobs, services and opportunity, and how they shape everyday life.

Role
Co-lead researcher and co-author (with Himig Reyes)
When
2023 · UC San Diego
Team
Johan Fernandez and Himig Reyes (executive summary, introduction, methodology); Erliza Balaoing and Jackson Patten (literature review). Community partner: Logan Heights Community Development Corporation. Advising: Professor Mirle Rabinowitz Bussell and UGIA Jonathan Lalouz.
Status
Completed report
Methods
American Community Survey trend analysis (three 5-year periods), Census tract comparison against the City of San Diego, Literature review, Stakeholder interviews, Historical and government document review
Tools and data
ACS 5-year estimates (2005-2009, 2010-2014, 2017-2021), Census tract mapping

Five neighborhoods between three freeways

Greater Logan Heights sits in Southeastern San Diego, boxed in by Interstates 5, 15 and 94. As defined by the Logan Heights Community Development Corporation, it takes in five neighborhoods: Memorial, Stockton, Sherman Heights, Grant Hill and Logan Heights. It has deep cultural roots and strong community ties, but it has not shared in the region's growth.

Our question was how changes in housing and transportation infrastructure have shaped residents' access to jobs, services and other opportunities, and how they shape everyday life. Our argument was direct: a persistent pattern of disinvestment in housing and transportation has harmed the physical, social and economic health of the community.

I wrote the introduction and co-wrote the executive summary and methodology with Himig Reyes. We did the work in partnership with the Logan Heights CDC, which is leading development efforts in the neighborhood.

What research says about transit, housing and displacement

Our literature review, written by Erliza Balaoing and Jackson Patten, pulled together work on housing disinvestment, transit access and displacement. Four strands shaped how we read the data.

  • Transit and housing belong in the same plan. The Center for Transit-Oriented Development's 2014 guidebook for HUD shows that transportation is the second-largest household cost after housing, and that households in walkable places spend far less of their income on getting around.
  • Transit investment in Latino neighborhoods can help or displace. Gerardo Sandoval's national study of Latino immigrant neighborhoods, which included Logan Heights, found that the key to an equitable outcome is residents guiding the process and building on existing social, political and cultural assets.
  • Sidewalks are contested ground. Loukaitou-Sideris and Ehrenfeucht show that sidewalk rules and designs are negotiated between groups with unequal power, which is why planners must watch who the street is being designed for.
  • Fear of transit crime is not borne out everywhere. Billings, Leland and Swindell found that Charlotte's light rail did not raise crime around stations, and property crime fell after station locations were announced.

Six census tracts, three snapshots, fifteen years

We used American Community Survey 5-year estimates from three periods: 2005-2009, 2010-2014 and 2017-2021. That let us track change over roughly fifteen years rather than read a single snapshot.

We represented Greater Logan Heights with census tracts 39.01, 39.02, 40, 47, 48 and 49. Tracts 41 and 46 hold small slices of the northern neighborhood, but we left them out because they also contain areas outside it and would have distorted the picture.

We compared tracts with each other to see variation inside the community, and compared the combined tracts with the City of San Diego. Where the numbers needed context, we used interviews with people working on housing and transportation in the neighborhood, plus historical and government records.

  • Housing variables: median rent and home value, age of housing, tenure, units per structure, vacancy.
  • Transportation variables: means of transportation to work and travel time to work, for workers 16 and over.

Renters, not owners, and more cars: what the census shows

Housing is mostly rented, old and low-density. In the 2017-2021 data, 70.9% of occupied units were renter-occupied, compared with a near-even split citywide of about 53% renters. That share has held near 70% since 2005-2009, so renters here have had little path into ownership and the wealth it builds.

Costs vary sharply within the neighborhood. Median gross rent ranged from $1,264 in the lowest tract to $1,812 in the highest, against a citywide median of $1,611 in 2021. Structures are much older than the city average and often poorly maintained, and vacancy, while falling, has generally been higher than citywide.

Transportation has moved toward the car. Driving to work rose from 2005 to 2021, with a jump in 2017-2021, while transit, walking and biking declined. We also found few comfortable bus stop amenities, few PRONTO fare outlets for buying bus and trolley fares, and a lack of dedicated bike lanes.

Most workers had relatively short commutes in every period, with a spike in trips over 40 minutes in 2010-2014 that eased by 2017-2021.

  • Recommendation 1: invest in refurbishing existing homes, for both upkeep and structural safety.
  • Recommendation 2: build more housing at greater intensity across the neighborhood.
  • Recommendation 3: allow property subdivision to lower the barrier to home purchase and open paths to wealth building.
  • Alongside these, our project summary called for new affordable housing, better transit options and bike-friendly infrastructure.

What the census can't tell us, and what I would do next

The ACS is sample data. Margins of error for small tracts can be large, and hard-to-reach groups, including many minority residents, can be undercounted. Our latest data was 2021, two years behind the report.

Our interviews were used selectively, not as a systematic survey, so the report leans on census trends more than on residents' own accounts. The recommendations focus on housing; the transportation findings deserve their own set of fixes.

Next, I would add the 2018-2022 and later ACS releases, map transit stop amenities and bike lanes directly, and pair the census work with structured resident interviews. I would also test whether new density can be added without the displacement Sandoval warns about.

Case studies

  • Barrio Logan, San Diego, CAChicano Park

    In April 1970 residents occupied land under the Coronado Bridge after learning the city planned a Highway Patrol station there, and won a park. The area had been cut apart by I-5, the bridge and industrial rezoning; the park is now a National Historic Landmark.

    Lesson for this project: Infrastructure decisions made over residents' heads have shaped this part of San Diego for decades, and organized residents have changed the outcome before.

    Source
  • Oakland, CAFruitvale Transit Village

    When BART proposed a large commuter parking structure at Fruitvale station in 1991, the Unity Council, a local Latino community development corporation, pushed back and led a mixed-use village instead, with mixed-income housing, a clinic, library, senior center, retail and a plaza linking the station to the main street.

    Lesson for this project: A neighborhood CDC, like the Logan Heights CDC, can turn a transit investment into housing and services for existing residents.

    Source
  • Los Angeles, Oakland and San Diego, CAEquitable TOD in Latino immigrant neighborhoods

    Gerardo Sandoval studied MacArthur Park, Boyle Heights, Fruitvale and Logan Heights, and found that transit-oriented development can strengthen Latino neighborhoods when residents guide it, for example through Boyle Heights' Mariachi Plaza and Logan Heights' Chicano Park muralists.

    Lesson for this project: Our density recommendation needs community control and cultural placemaking built in to avoid displacing the residents it aims to help.

    Source

Sources

  2. Sandoval, G. (2017). Developing a Model for Transit-Oriented Development in Latino Immigrant Communities (project brief). National Institute for Transportation and Communities. Link
  3. Billings, S. B., Leland, S., and Swindell, D. (2011). The effects of the announcement and opening of light rail transit stations on neighborhood crime. Journal of Urban Affairs. Link
  4. Loukaitou-Sideris, A., and Ehrenfeucht, R. (2009). Sidewalks: Conflict and Negotiation over Public Space. MIT Press. Link
  5. Smithsonian Magazine (2020). Fifty years ago, fed up with the city's neglect, a San Diego community rose up to create Chicano Park. Link
  6. Benfield, K. (2011). The remarkable story of Oakland's Fruitvale Transit Village. Sustainable Cities Collective. Link

Community and equity research · UC San Diego · USP 138

City Heights: People and Needs

A neighborhood needs assessment of City Heights, San Diego, focused on high school graduation, with proposals for senior care and cultural programs.

A young neighborhood, two high schools behind the city

City Heights is young. Its median age in the 2020 Census was 31.7, against 36.3 for San Diego County. It is home to 76,624 residents and many immigrant and refugee families, and about 63% of residents speak a language other than English at home.

Its two high schools trail the city. San Diego's average graduation rate was 91%. Hoover High graduated 83% and Crawford High 85%. Among adults in the neighborhood, about 42% had less than a high school diploma. Research on dropping out describes it as a process, not an event, with warning signs along the way.

With Joshua Lee and Jaehee Nam, I asked what high school students in City Heights need, and how those needs could be met to improve their academic outcomes and future opportunities.

Role
Team member (with Joshua Lee and Jaehee Nam)
When
UC San Diego · USP 138
Team
Joshua Lee, Jaehee Nam and Johan Fernandez, for USP 138 (Anderson).
Status
Completed report
Methods
Demographic profile from census and forecast data, School performance comparison, Literature and policy review, Program proposals
Tools and data
2020 U.S. Census, U.S. Census Bureau time series, U.S. News & World Report high school data

What City Heights high school students need

What are the educational needs and challenges of high school students in City Heights, San Diego, and how could they be addressed to improve academic outcomes and future opportunities?

City Heights is one of San Diego's most diverse and youngest neighborhoods, and home to many immigrant and refugee families. With Joshua Lee and Jaehee Nam, I built a needs assessment that started with who lives there and moved to what the neighborhood lacks.

Education was our lead need. We also looked at senior medical needs and at cultural needs, because those shape the same households.

Why high school completion comes first

Two pieces of outside research frame why high school completion is the right place to start.

  • Dropping out is a process, not an event. Russell Rumberger, director of the California Dropout Research Project, has argued that there are warning signs along the way, with middle and high school failure the best predictors.
  • Place-based programs and school quality are different levers. Dobbie and Fryer's lottery study of the Harlem Children's Zone Promise Academy found large math gains, and the evidence pointed to the school itself, not the surrounding community programs, as the driver.

Census profiles and a two-school comparison

We built a demographic profile from the 2020 Census, Census Bureau trends and a 2025 ethnicity forecast. We compared the two City Heights high schools with the San Diego average using graduation rates, enrollment and college readiness scores, and drew on published research on the costs of dropping out.

For each need we proposed programs aimed at the specific gap we found.

Young, multilingual and behind on graduation

City Heights had 76,624 residents in the 2020 Census, with 3.04 persons per household. The median age was 31.7, against 36.3 for San Diego County. About 63% of residents speak a language other than English at home, mostly Spanish and Vietnamese. The 2025 forecast put the population at about 52% Hispanic, 18% Asian, 15% white and 11% Black.

Education levels were low: about 42% of adults had less than a high school diploma, and only 15% held a bachelor's degree or higher.

Both high schools trailed the city. Against a San Diego average graduation rate of 91%, Hoover High (2,147 students in grades 9-12) graduated 83% and Crawford High (1,117 students) 85%. College readiness scores were 33.7 at Hoover and 27.4 at Crawford, against a city average of about 38.

The senior share of residents rose from 5.8% in 2000 to 9.7% in 2019, raising needs for primary care, home health, transportation and culturally and linguistically appropriate services. We also noted that immigrant families often lose native-language fluency by the third generation.

  • Education proposals: an English language program for all ages, after-school tutoring, and a high school recreation program to address academic and peer disconnection.
  • Cultural proposals: weekend language schools with proficiency tests usable for college credit, night markets featuring Vietnamese, Somali, Cambodian, Laotian and Latino cultures with entry fees funding the language schools, guest speakers in high schools, recognition of holidays such as Tet, Eid al-Fitr and Day of the Dead, and a museum of the neighborhood's ethnic communities.

A desk study, and what I would do next

This was a desk study. We did not survey or interview students, families or teachers, so the needs are inferred from data rather than heard directly. Graduation rates and readiness scores are single snapshots for two schools.

Our proposals were not costed or matched to existing programs in the neighborhood, and City Heights already has deep education partnerships.

Next, I would map where students live relative to their schools and after-school options, interview students and counselors at Hoover and Crawford, and check each proposal against what partners already run before adding anything new.

Case studies

  • City Heights, San Diego, CACity Heights Educational Collaborative

    Since 1998, San Diego State University, San Diego Unified, the teachers' association and Price Charities have partnered with Rosa Parks Elementary, Monroe Clark Middle and Hoover High. The College Avenue Compact (2007) guaranteed SDSU admission to qualifying students, and Hoover graduates enrolling at SDSU rose from 20 in fall 2005 to 57 planned for fall 2009.

    Lesson for this project: Any new program in City Heights should build on this K-12 to college pipeline rather than duplicate it.

    Source
  • New York, NYHarlem Children's Zone Promise Academy

    A lottery-based evaluation by Dobbie and Fryer found Promise Academy middle school students scored 0.28 standard deviations higher in math than students who lost the lottery, with gains traced to the school rather than the neighborhood programs.

    Lesson for this project: Tutoring and recreation are worth doing, but the biggest gains may come from what happens inside Hoover and Crawford themselves.

    Source

Sources

  2. Dobbie, W., and Fryer, R. High-Quality Schools and Achievement Among the Poor in the United States. J-PAL evaluation summary. Link
  3. Alliance for Excellent Education (2008). Straight A's: Public Education Policy and Progress, 8(17), reporting Russell Rumberger, California Dropout Research Project. Link

Community and equity research · 2023 · UC San Diego

Revelle Plaza: Green Space and Student Well-Being

A mixed-methods study of how students use and judge one of UC San Diego's oldest open spaces, and a proposed plan to scale it into a campus green space redesign.

Open space is not the same as used space

Revelle Plaza sits at the center of UC San Diego's first college. It is one of the oldest open spaces on campus. Universities have plenty of space like it, but much of it goes unused when it gives students nothing to do there.

That matters for more than looks. In Auckland, more usable green space within 3 km was associated with lower treatment rates for anxiety and mood disorders. In Wisconsin, a study of 2,479 residents tied more neighborhood green space to fewer symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress. And in New York, William H. Whyte showed that seating, sun, food and other people decide where a crowd gathers.

So we went to the plaza to count, ask and listen. We tallied students by zone across three time periods, surveyed them and ran short interviews. This pilot asks how the design and layout of a green space shape whether students use it and how they feel there.

Role
Researcher (with Ethan Lee and Karina Wong)
When
2023 · UC San Diego
Team
Ethan Lee and Karina Wong. Advisor: Professor Amy Lerner.
Status
Pilot
Methods
Observational counts across three time periods, Student surveys (open-ended), Short structured interviews, Literature review
Tools and data
Behavioral mapping of key plaza zones, Survey and interview instruments

Why Revelle Plaza, and what we asked

Universities have plenty of open space, but much of it goes unused when it gives students nothing to do there. Revelle Plaza, at the center of UC San Diego's first college, is one of the oldest open spaces on campus.

We asked how green space design and layout affect whether students use a space and how they feel, and which design strategies could raise engagement and satisfaction. Revelle Plaza was our test case.

I worked on the study with Ethan Lee and Karina Wong, with guidance from Professor Amy Lerner.

Green space and the mind: the research behind it

The study rests on a well-established link between green space and mental health, and on a shorter line of work about what makes a plaza get used.

  • Access to green space is linked to better mental health. Nutsford, Pearson and Kingham (2013) found in Auckland that more usable green space within 3 km, and a shorter distance to the nearest one, were associated with lower treatment rates for anxiety and mood disorders.
  • The link holds at the neighborhood scale. Beyer and colleagues (2014) studied 2,479 Wisconsin residents and found that more neighborhood green space went with fewer symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress.
  • Nature helps people recover from mental fatigue. Stephen Kaplan's attention restoration framework (1995) explains why time in natural settings can restore the focus that study and work drain, which matters on a campus.
  • Design details decide use. William H. Whyte's observations of New York plazas showed that what draws people most is other people, and that seating, sun and food shape where they gather.

Counting, asking, listening: how we studied the plaza

We used a mixed-methods design so that counts and opinions could check each other.

Observational counts tallied the number of students in several key areas of the plaza across three time periods, to see which zones drew people and when. Short interviews asked a series of yes/no questions and closed with an open prompt on what students would improve. Surveys used open-ended questions about students' experiences and habits in the plaza.

  • Observation: total counts by plaza zone, three time periods.
  • Interviews: yes/no items plus one open improvement prompt.
  • Surveys: open-ended questions on experience and behavior.

A field method and a bigger plan: what came out of it

The pilot produced a field method for reading one plaza: where students cluster, when the space empties, and what they say is missing. The detailed counts and response themes are not yet written up in a form I can publish here.

From the pilot, I drafted a proposed plan to test the same question at campus scale. Everything below is a plan with target numbers, not a result.

  • Proposed: a literature review of 50 or more scholarly articles on green space design and student well-being.
  • Proposed: an online survey of 1,200 students and 15 focus groups, analyzed with statistics and thematic coding.
  • Proposed: a redesign of about 10,000 square feet of campus space into distinct zones for quiet study, physical activity and social time, developed with landscape architects, students, faculty and campus facilities.
  • Proposed: a post-implementation survey and focus groups with 800 students.
  • Target outcomes set in the proposal: a 35% increase in green space use and a 25% improvement in student-reported well-being. These are goals to test, not findings.

One plaza, a few time periods: limits and next steps

The pilot looked at one plaza, at a few time periods, with a convenience sample of students. It can show patterns of use, not prove that design changes well-being.

The proposed scale-up names its own hurdles: reaching a representative mix of students, physical limits of existing spaces, administrative approval and cost.

Next, I would publish the pilot counts and survey themes, then run a before-and-after comparison around even a small change, such as movable seating or shade, before attempting a 10,000 square foot redesign. A comparison plaza that does not change would make the result far more convincing.

Case studies

  • New York, NYBryant Park restoration

    Once avoided and overrun by drug dealing, Bryant Park was redesigned starting in the 1980s on William H. Whyte's advice: lowered toward street level, hedges and fences removed, more entrances added, and thousands of movable chairs introduced. It now draws about 25,000 visitors a day in warm months.

    Lesson for this project: Small, cheap moves such as sightlines, entrances and movable seating can change how a plaza is used without rebuilding it.

    Source
  • New York, NYStreet Life Project

    Starting in 1969, Whyte and his assistants used time-lapse film and direct observation to record how people actually used plazas and streets, published as The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces (1980). The method became the basis of the Project for Public Spaces.

    Lesson for this project: Systematic counts by zone and time, the core of our Revelle method, are a proven way to judge public space before redesigning it.

    Source

Sources

  1. Nutsford, D., Pearson, A. L., and Kingham, S. (2013). An ecological study investigating the association between access to urban green space and mental health. Public Health, 127(11), 1005-1011. Link
  2. Beyer, K. M. M., Kaltenbach, A., Szabo, A., Bogar, S., Nieto, F. J., and Malecki, K. M. (2014). Exposure to neighborhood green space and mental health: evidence from the Survey of the Health of Wisconsin. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 11(3), 3453-3472. Link
  3. Kaplan, S. (1995). The restorative benefits of nature: toward an integrative framework. Journal of Environmental Psychology, 15(3), 169-182. Link
  4. Project for Public Spaces. William H. Whyte. Link
  5. American Planning Association (2010). Bryant Park, New York, New York. Great Places in America. Link

GIS and spatial technology · Feb 2023 – Mar 2024 · UC San Diego Facilities Management

Georeferencing CAD Files for UC San Diego Campus Buildings

Placing 1,788 campus building drawings on the map, with world files and a QA checklist, so UC San Diego's facilities data could live in one shared spatial frame.

1,788 drawings that floated in space

UC San Diego keeps floor plans for buildings across the La Jolla East and West campuses, Scripps Institution of Oceanography and UC San Diego Health. Each drawing was precise on its own terms. Yet each sat in its own local coordinate space. Nothing tied a room in one file to a street, a utility line or a building in another.

That matters more than it sounds. Decisions about which buildings get maintenance, which rooms get reassigned and where new work is routed depend on data people can trust and line up. A drawing that floats in space cannot enter that conversation.

From February 2023 to March 2024, Kushinga Pfende and I worked through 1,788 of these files, one control point at a time. The question was whether we could anchor the whole building stock to the campus GIS in a way someone else could check, repeat and extend.

Role
GIS Project Assistant (with Kushinga Pfende)
When
Feb 2023 – Mar 2024 · UC San Diego Facilities Management
Team
Kushinga Pfende (GIS student collaborator), Diana Henderson (project supervisor), Sung Lee (GIS Analyst, CAD library and control points)
Status
Completed
Methods
Control-point georeferencing, World file creation, Spreadsheet-based QA/QC checklist, Multi-campus data integration
Tools and data
ArcGIS, CAD floor plan library, Campus GIS spatial database, Facilities spreadsheet

Drawings without a place: the question

UC San Diego keeps a large library of CAD drawings: floor plans and layouts for buildings on the La Jolla East and West campuses, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, UC San Diego Health and other sites. Each drawing was precise on its own terms but sat in its own local coordinate space. Nothing tied a room in one file to a street, a utility line or a building in another.

The question was practical. Could we anchor every drawing to real-world coordinates so the whole building stock could be viewed, measured and queried alongside the rest of the campus GIS? And could we do it in a way that someone else could check, repeat and extend?

This matters beyond tidy maps. Decisions about which buildings get maintenance, which rooms get reassigned and where new work is routed depend on data that people can trust and line up. A drawing that floats in space cannot enter that conversation.

Control points and digital twins: the research behind it

The method follows Esri's documented workflow for CAD data. A spatial reference is assigned first, the drawing is moved, rotated and scaled into place, and control points pair features in the drawing with the same features on the map. The result is saved to a world file that ArcGIS reads each time the drawing loads.

The wider literature treats this kind of work as groundwork for campus digital twins. Meschini and colleagues (2022) built a BIM-GIS asset management system for the University of Turin, a university spread across many sites, and found that georeferencing the whole building stock was the step that let scattered departmental records become one relational database.

  • Esri: control points define the transformation, and a spatial reference is required for it to be accurate.
  • Esri: a CAD world file stores point pairs describing a 2D transformation and needs a matching .prj file for the coordinate system.
  • Esri also notes that the best CAD-GIS workflows avoid world files entirely by drawing in geospatial coordinates from the start.
  • Meschini et al. (2022): a georeferenced building stock is the base layer for a multi-site university digital twin.

Point by point, row by row: how we did it

Kushinga Pfende and I worked from the CAD library that Facilities keeps on OneDrive. Sung Lee helped compile the library and the control points. Diana Henderson supervised and guided the methodology and ArcGIS workflow.

We brought the drawings into ArcGIS and converted them to a geodatabase format. For each drawing we linked recognizable features, such as survey markers, road intersections, sidewalks and other landmarks, to their known locations in the campus GIS spatial database. Those control points set where the drawing sits, how it is rotated and how it scales.

I also built a georeferencing checklist from a facilities spreadsheet the university provided. It already listed facility number, name, total floors, floor plan IDs and area. I added columns for georeferencing status, comments and a needs-review flag, then worked through every row.

  • For multi-floor buildings, I checked that the floor plan IDs matched the stated number of floors.
  • For each building, I recorded the coordinate system, units, origin coordinates, scale and rotation angle from the world file parameters.
  • Once every file was georeferenced, I filtered for rows flagged for re-review, so adjustment work had a clear queue.

1,788 files on one map: what we produced

The main deliverable was 1,788 georeferenced CAD files, each with a world file holding its coordinate information. Building drawings from across UC San Diego's campuses could now be overlaid on the campus basemap and analyzed with other GIS layers.

The checklist became a quality assurance tool. It shows which buildings still need adjustment to reach survey-grade alignment with the campus basemap, and it was set up to guide and validate CAD mapping for new campus projects going forward.

Together these give Facilities a common spatial frame for classrooms, offices and other assets. That is the starting point for asset tracking, measurement and the 3D visualization that a campus digital twin needs.

World files are a patch: limits and next steps

World files fix the symptom, not the cause. Each new or revised drawing made in local coordinates will need the same treatment, which is why Esri recommends drawing in real coordinates from the start. A next step would be a CAD standard for new campus projects that requires a known coordinate system.

We did not record a formal accuracy measure, such as residual error per control point, in the checklist. Adding it would let the needs-review flag rest on a threshold instead of judgment, and would make the survey-grade goal testable.

Finally, georeferenced drawings are still drawings. The next layer of value comes from turning them into structured features (rooms, uses, occupants) that can answer questions about how space is shared across departments and campuses.

Case studies

  • Turin, ItalyUniversity of Turin BIM-GIS asset management

    Researchers georeferenced the university's entire, geographically scattered building stock and linked BIM models into a GIS-based web platform with dashboards and a unified relational database.

    Lesson for this project: Georeferencing every building is the step that lets fragmented departmental records become one campus-wide asset system.

    Source
  • Seattle, WashingtonUniversity of Washington automated indoor mapping

    UW Facilities built automated FME workflows that convert AutoCAD floor plans into a geodatabase on a schedule, covering about 1,700 floors and 24 million square feet of interior space.

    Lesson for this project: Once drawings are georeferenced, automating the CAD-to-GIS update keeps the campus map current without repeating manual work.

    Source
  • Amherst, MassachusettsUMass Amherst indoor asset mapping

    UMass Amherst moved its asset inventory indoors using georeferenced CAD floor plans and 360-degree photos in ArcGIS Pro, with a longer-term aim of a pedestrian accessibility network.

    Lesson for this project: Georeferenced floor plans open the door to indoor questions, such as accessibility, that outdoor maps cannot answer.

    Source

Sources

  2. Esri. World files for CAD and BIM data. ArcGIS Pro 3.2 documentation. Link
  3. Meschini, S., Pellegrini, L., Locatelli, M., Accardo, D., Tagliabue, L. C., Di Giuda, G. M., and Avena, M. (2022). Toward cognitive digital twins using a BIM-GIS asset management system for a diffused university. Frontiers in Built Environment, 8. Link
  4. Safe Software. The University of Washington automates indoor mapping process. Customer story. Link
  5. Wrenner, R., and Okscin, A. (2018). Facilities track: Mapping a university inside and out. NEARC Fall 2018. Link

GIS and spatial technology · Sep 2023 – Mar 2024 · UC San Diego Facilities Management

UC San Diego Drone Flight Initiative

Building a compliant drone-mapping workflow for campus planning, from DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise flights to orthomosaics and 3D terrain models in ArcGIS.

A drone, a rulebook and a campus map

Ask what a UC San Diego building site looks like today, and the basemap may answer with a picture that is months or years old. Satellite and aerial imagery is often too coarse for site work. Walking the site and taking notes is slow and hard to compare over time.

A drone can fill that gap, but only as one link in a longer chain. Under FAA Part 107, pilots need a remote pilot certificate, flights stay below 400 feet and in visual line of sight, and controlled airspace needs authorization. Accuracy depends on where ground control points go, not only on the software. Then the imagery still has to reach the GIS that Facilities already uses.

From September 2023 to March 2024, I led a pilot with DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise drones across UC San Diego's colleges. It tested whether a small team could fly safely and legally, process the imagery into accurate products, and get those products into the hands of campus planners.

Role
GIS Project Assistant, initiative lead
When
Sep 2023 – Mar 2024 · UC San Diego Facilities Management
Status
Pilot
Methods
UAS flight planning and operations, Photogrammetry, Orthomosaic and 3D terrain model production, Equipment evaluation, Regulatory compliance review
Tools and data
DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise, ArcGIS Drone2Map, Pix4D, Agisoft Metashape, ArcGIS Online

Old basemaps, slow site walks: the question

Campus planners at UC San Diego need current pictures of the ground: what was built, what changed, and what needs attention. Satellite and aerial basemaps are often months or years old and too coarse for site work. Walking a site and taking notes is slow and hard to compare over time.

I led a campus-wide initiative to test whether drones could fill that gap for infrastructure planning, environmental monitoring and sustainability analysis. The working question was simple. Could a small team fly safely and legally, process the imagery into accurate products, and get those products into the GIS that Facilities already uses?

Answering it meant treating the drone as one piece of a longer chain. Flight rules, camera settings, processing choices and data storage all affect whether an image ends up useful to a planner.

Ground control and the FAA: the research behind it

Drone photogrammetry turns overlapping photos into orthomosaics, point clouds and terrain models. How accurate those products are depends heavily on ground control points (GCPs), marked locations measured independently on the ground. Ferrer-González and colleagues (2020) tested GCP counts and layouts and found that placement matters as much as quantity: points spread alternately on both sides of a corridor beat other layouts with the same or more points.

Flying on a campus is also a regulated activity. Under the FAA's Part 107 rules, commercial and institutional pilots need a remote pilot certificate, registered aircraft that broadcast Remote ID, flights below 400 feet with the drone in visual line of sight, and airspace authorization (for example through LAANC) in controlled airspace. Night flights, flights over people and beyond-line-of-sight work need waivers.

Universities are also starting to treat drones as shared infrastructure rather than one-off projects. In March 2026 the University of Arizona launched an Integrated Aerial Operations program that routes every campus drone flight request through one coordination center, covering facilities inspections, parking analysis and geospatial mapping under FAA rules and university policy.

  • Accuracy is earned in the field, through GCP layout, not only in the software.
  • Compliance is part of the workflow, not paperwork after it: airspace, people on the ground and pilot certification shape where and when you can fly.

Four objectives, three processing tools: how I did it

I used DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise drones to capture high-resolution imagery across UC San Diego's colleges. Every flight was planned to meet FAA Part 107 and UC San Diego Environment, Health and Safety (EH&S) requirements.

I processed the imagery in ArcGIS Drone2Map and Pix4D, with Agisoft Metashape also in the toolset, and published results through ArcGIS Online. Running more than one processing package let me compare how each handled the same campus data.

The initiative had four objectives: set up a complete drone-mapping workflow for campus planning, bring aerial data into GIS asset-management systems, keep every flight compliant with FAA and EH&S rules, and give hands-on training in photogrammetry and flight operations.

Training was part of the design from the start. The goal was not one skilled pilot but a workflow that others in Facilities could learn, repeat and check, from flight planning through processing and publishing.

Orthomosaics, terrain models and a buying guide: what came out of it

We produced orthomosaic basemaps and 3D terrain models for campus planners and sustainability teams. On the project's own accounting, site inspections became more than 60 percent more efficient.

I created a Drone Model Comparison Matrix to guide equipment purchases, so future buying decisions could rest on documented tradeoffs instead of brand familiarity.

I also proposed a Drone Data Hub for UC San Diego Facilities Management and the RMP divisions. The hub is a proposal: a shared home where flights, imagery and derived products could be found and reused instead of living on individual drives.

  • Orthomosaic basemaps for planners
  • 3D terrain models for sustainability teams
  • Drone Model Comparison Matrix
  • Proposed Drone Data Hub

Checking the 60 percent: limits and next steps

The 60 percent efficiency figure is the project's estimate, and I would want to document the baseline and the measure behind it before leaning on it. The same goes for accuracy: a formal check against surveyed checkpoints would show how far the orthomosaics can be trusted for design work and not only for planning.

Several next steps are planned but not done. They include vegetation and stormwater monitoring with multispectral sensors, change detection for construction and sustainability reporting, and AI-based feature extraction to build an infrastructure inventory.

Drones also raise questions that are not technical. Who is in the imagery, how long it is kept and who can see it are governance choices, and a Drone Data Hub would be the right place to write them down.

Case studies

  • Amherst, MassachusettsUMass Amherst campus UAS mapping

    In 2023 a UMass team mapped the 2.5-square-mile campus in roughly 600 m by 600 m blocks with DJI Mavic drones, using RTK-surveyed ground control points every 200 to 300 meters in the core campus to produce orthomosaics and point clouds for coordinating construction.

    Lesson for this project: A campus-wide program depends on a deliberate GCP plan, which is the clearest gap to close in a UC San Diego follow-up.

    Source
  • MinnesotaMnDOT drone bridge inspections

    The Minnesota Department of Transportation used drones on 39 bridges in 2015 and 2016 in place of under-bridge vehicles, rope access and scaffolding, with average cost savings of 40 percent and better deliverables even where costs did not fall.

    Lesson for this project: Inspection efficiency claims are strongest when they are tied to a specific baseline method and cost, which is the standard this project's efficiency figure should meet.

    Source
  • Chula Vista, CaliforniaChula Vista Police drone as first responder

    Starting in October 2018 under the FAA's UAS Integration Pilot Program, Chula Vista police launched drones to emergency calls from headquarters, operating within visual line of sight and under an FAA waiver for flights over people.

    Lesson for this project: A San Diego County program shows that scaling drone use depends on working with the FAA on waivers and on clear operating rules, the same foundation a campus Drone Data Hub would need.

    Source

GIS and spatial technology · UC San Diego

ArcGIS Indoors Pilot for UC San Diego

Turning existing CAD floor plans into a floor-aware Indoors dataset and using field forms to map safety elements inside campus buildings.

Most campus maps stop at the front door

Walk into a campus building and the map runs out. The information that matters in an emergency, such as where safety equipment is and how floors connect, usually lives in paper plans, PDFs or someone's memory.

Researchers who study emergency response describe the same gap. GIS supports dispatch well outdoors, but indoor navigation remains underdeveloped. Mahdaviparsa and McCuen worked with a fire marshal's team to judge which indoor maps first responders could read under pressure.

UC San Diego already held part of the answer. Its CAD floor plans show walls, doors and rooms in detail. I came to ArcGIS Indoors with no prior exposure and learned it through the Esri Training Academy. This pilot asks whether those existing plans can become a floor-aware indoor map, with safety elements collected in the field and shown in a viewer people could use.

Role
Pilot developer (data model, field forms, viewer configuration)
When
UC San Diego
Status
Pilot
Methods
CAD-to-Indoors data conversion, Field data collection with survey forms, Indoor web viewer configuration, Self-directed technical training
Tools and data
ArcGIS Pro (Indoors toolbox), ArcGIS Field Maps, ArcGIS Indoors Viewer, CAD floor plans

Maps that end at the door: the question

Most campus maps stop at the front door. Once you are inside a building, the information that matters in an emergency, such as where safety equipment is and how floors connect, usually lives in paper plans, PDFs or someone's memory.

This pilot asked whether UC San Diego's existing CAD floor plans could become a working indoor map. Specifically, could I build a floor-aware dataset from those plans, collect the locations of safety elements inside buildings of interest, and show the result in a viewer people could use?

CAD floor plans were the natural starting point. The university already maintains them, they show walls, doors and rooms in detail, and they can be reused instead of redrawn.

Sites, levels and units: the research behind it

ArcGIS Indoors is built on a published information model. It organizes indoor space as a hierarchy of sites, facilities (building footprints), levels (floors), units (rooms and other spaces) and details (walls, doors and windows), with optional pathways and transitions for routing between rooms and floors. Esri provides tools to import CAD floor plans directly into that schema.

Indoor maps matter most when people cannot see where they are going. Mahdaviparsa and McCuen (2019) compared methods for building indoor networks from BIM and CAD data for emergency response, and worked with a fire marshal's team to judge which ones first responders could read under pressure. Their starting point is the same gap this pilot targets: GIS supports dispatch well outdoors, but indoor navigation remains underdeveloped.

Universities that have adopted Indoors at scale describe the same path. The University of Rhode Island moved floor plans from a proprietary facility management system to CAD standards and then into the Indoors model, and its public safety staff now use those floor plans for emergency management and event coordination.

  • A shared data model means a pilot built on a few buildings can grow to a campus without redesign.
  • Safety use cases set a high bar for clarity: data has to be easy to read in a stressful moment, not just complete.

From CAD to Field Maps to viewer: how I built it

I imported existing CAD floor plans into an Indoors dataset created with the Indoors toolbox in ArcGIS Pro. That produced the layered structure the Indoors model expects, with levels, units, details and facility features.

I then created and managed survey forms in ArcGIS Field Maps and used them to record the locations of safety elements inside the buildings of interest. Collecting in the field, inside the building, ties each point to the right floor and room instead of guessing from a drawing.

Toward the end of the project I experimented with configuring the ArcGIS Indoors Viewer for our campus data, so the floor plans and collected points could be browsed floor by floor.

Each step fed the next. Clean floor plans made the levels and units usable as a base map in Field Maps, and well-placed field points made the viewer worth opening.

A working dataset and a steep learning curve: what came out of it

The pilot produced a working Indoors dataset built from campus CAD plans, a set of Field Maps survey forms for safety-element collection, field-collected safety element locations for the buildings of interest, and a first configuration of the Indoors Viewer.

Just as useful was what the process taught. I had no exposure to ArcGIS Indoors before this project, and all of my training came from the Esri Training Academy and Esri's own video documentation of the product.

The work was highly iterative. Many early iterations used data outside our area of interest, and narrowing the scope was part of learning how the Indoors model and its tools behave.

Scope first, responders next: limits and next steps

This was a pilot, and the viewer configuration was experimental. It covered selected buildings, not the campus, and it did not include routing or occupant data.

The early scoping problems point to a clear lesson: define the area of interest and the safety element list before importing anything. A short data dictionary agreed with campus safety staff would make the field forms consistent and the results easier to maintain.

Next, I would test the viewer with the people who would use it in an emergency, as Mahdaviparsa and McCuen did with fire service staff, and set up a routine for updating the indoor data when floor plans or equipment change.

Finally, safety data inside buildings raises access questions. Deciding who can see equipment locations, and whether the map should be public, internal or shared only with responders, is a policy choice the campus would need to make before going further.

Case studies

  • Rhode IslandUniversity of Rhode Island smart campus

    URI began an ArcGIS Indoors pilot in 2022, migrated floor plans from a legacy facility management system to CAD standards and then to the Indoors model, and now uses Indoors floor plans for public safety, emergency management and event coordination.

    Lesson for this project: A pilot like this one can grow into a campus-wide safety and operations tool once floor plans are standardized and an owner is in place.

    Source
  • New Jersey (Rutgers University)Rutgers Lucy Stone Hall indoor map

    A Rutgers geography student converted CAD floor plans for a famously confusing building into ArcGIS layers with rooms, doors, stairwells and elevators, added turn-by-turn wayfinding, and presented it to campus planning and operations as a proof of concept in 2023.

    Lesson for this project: A small, well-scoped student pilot can be enough to show campus decision makers what indoor GIS can do.

    Source

GIS and spatial technology · Nov 2024 – Apr 2026 · Action Research

Stormwater Planning and Compliance

Helping Orange County cities meet California's MS4 stormwater permit through coordinated workflows, GIS dashboards, outreach campaigns and a regional study of utility vault pump-out reporting.

Rain, runoff and four cities in step

When it rains in Southern California, the runoff picks up pesticides, oil and trash from streets and yards. It flows through storm drains into creeks and the ocean. No single pipe is to blame. The pollution comes from everyday behavior spread across thousands of properties.

That makes compliance a coordination problem. The San Diego Region's MS4 permit alone covers 39 agencies. Proving that outreach works is hard too. A 2022 Washington State University synthesis found that only 13 percent of studies on stormwater behavior change campaigns used a control group.

At Action Research I worked across four Orange County municipalities with dashboards, templates and outreach campaigns. The question behind the work was practical. How can several agencies run stormwater programs that line up with each other, show their progress clearly and actually change what residents and businesses do?

Role
Project & Program Associate, Action Research
When
Nov 2024 – Apr 2026 · Action Research
Status
Completed
Methods
Multi-jurisdictional program coordination, GIS dashboards and project tracking, Outreach campaign design and evaluation, Inter-agency interviews, Process assessment and recommendations
Tools and data
ArcGIS Online, Power BI, Excel, Smartsheet, Adobe Creative Suite, Microsoft Teams

Pollution from many hands: the question

When it rains in Southern California, runoff carries whatever is on the ground, including pesticides, oil and trash, through storm drains and into creeks and the ocean. Cities and counties are responsible for reducing that pollution under California's Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System (MS4) permits.

Most of the pollution comes from everyday behavior spread across thousands of properties, so compliance is as much about coordination and outreach as about pipes. At Action Research I led multi-jurisdictional projects that asked a practical question: how can several agencies run stormwater programs that line up with each other, show their progress clearly and actually change what residents and businesses do?

Permits, regions and proof: the research behind it

Under the Clean Water Act's NPDES program, the EPA requires operators of municipal separate storm sewer systems to hold permits and run stormwater management programs, with public education and outreach as one required element. In California, Regional Water Boards issue these permits. Orange County is split between two regions: the Santa Ana Region permit for north and central Orange County, and the San Diego Region's regional MS4 permit (Order R9-2013-0001, as amended), which covers 39 agencies across San Diego County and parts of Orange and Riverside counties and requires Water Quality Improvement Plans for each watershed.

The EPA describes nonpoint source pollution, the runoff-driven kind from lawns, streets and homes, as the leading remaining cause of water quality problems. Because it comes from many hands, outreach is a core tool, but its effect is hard to prove. A 2022 Washington State University synthesis of stormwater behavior change campaigns found that about 57 percent of studies with baseline data reported successful adoption of the target behavior, while only 13 percent used a control group.

  • Permits set the requirements, but the work happens across many cities with different staff and systems.
  • Outreach works best when it targets a concrete behavior, such as pesticide use, and measures that behavior, not just awareness.

Dashboards, templates and campaigns: how we did it

I worked with planners, engineers and communications specialists to support city and county agencies across Orange County in carrying out their MS4 programs. My role was to connect regulatory data to planning tools that staff could act on.

I coordinated planning and compliance workflows across four municipalities so that community outreach lined up with each city's local planning objectives. I built GIS dashboards and project tracking systems that showed site activities, compliance metrics and public participation outcomes in one place.

I also set up standardized project governance templates to improve QA/QC, communication between departments and contract reporting. On the outreach side, I supported the design and evaluation of campaigns including Good, Bad and Bugly, HOA binder updates and pesticide reduction efforts.

Tracing vault pump-outs: the TO39 subproject

For the County of San Diego's Watershed Protection Department, I conducted a regional assessment of how utility vault pump-outs are reported. When utilities pump water out of underground vaults, that discharge can enter the storm drain system, and inconsistent reporting makes it hard to track.

I evaluated the protocols between municipal stormwater systems and public utilities, mapped contact coverage and infrastructure locations for possible GIS integration, and summarized inter-agency interviews into a formal deliverable for the department. The work closed with recommendations for process improvements that link environmental compliance with planning documentation under the County's NPDES obligations.

Working tools, not a single report: what came out of it

The main products were working tools rather than a single report: GIS dashboards and tracking systems for site activity and compliance, standardized governance templates used across projects, and outreach materials and campaign evaluations for residents and HOAs.

The TO39 study produced a formal deliverable for the County of San Diego's Watershed Protection Department, a map of contact coverage and infrastructure locations, and recommendations to make pump-out reporting more consistent and transparent.

Across both, the goal was the same: reduce nonpoint source pollution and connect public works and stormwater efforts to wider regional sustainability and development goals.

Proving behavior change: limits and next steps

The hardest part of stormwater outreach is showing that it worked. Participation and reach are easy to count, but the research shows few campaigns measure behavior against a control group. A next step would be to pair a campaign like pesticide reduction with before-and-after behavior surveys in matched neighborhoods.

Coordination across jurisdictions also depends on shared data. Each agency keeps records in its own systems, and the dashboards are only as good as what flows into them. The TO39 recommendations point toward common reporting formats and GIS integration as the durable fix.

There is also an equity question I would like to study: whether outreach reaches renters, non-English speakers and neighborhoods without HOAs as well as it reaches organized homeowners.

Case studies

  • San Diego County, CaliforniaProject Clean Water

    The 21 San Diego Region stormwater copermittees run a shared regional clearinghouse covering watershed management areas from South Orange County to the Tijuana River, with joint outreach such as 52 Ways to Love H2O and youth Stormwater Stewards programs.

    Lesson for this project: A regional clearinghouse gives many agencies one public face and one set of resources, which is the kind of coordination multi-city compliance needs.

    Source
  • Orange County, CaliforniaH2OC, the Orange County Stormwater Program

    H2OC publishes shared pollution prevention materials for residents and businesses on topics like runoff, landscaping, pet care and household hazardous waste, many in Spanish, Vietnamese, Korean and Chinese.

    Lesson for this project: Shared, multilingual materials let individual cities reach more residents without each building their own campaign from scratch.

    Source
  • Los Angeles County, CaliforniaSafe, Clean Water Program

    Approved by voters in 2018, the program funds stormwater capture and water quality projects through municipal, regional and district shares, and tracks projects through a public online map portal.

    Lesson for this project: Dedicated funding plus a public project map makes stormwater investment visible, a model for the tracking dashboards in this project.

    Source

Urban technology and policy · Senior thesis · UC San Diego Urban Expo

Defining A.I. Urban Dynamics: The Role of A.I. Urban Intelligence

My senior thesis asked how cities are bringing artificial intelligence into planning, and what governance, transparency and inclusion should look like when they do. It placed 3rd at the UC San Diego Urban Expo.

When an algorithm decides where attention goes

An algorithm that routes inspections, ranks requests or flags risk looks like a technical tool. It is also a decision about how public attention and resources are allocated. Cities are starting to use artificial intelligence and machine learning in planning and public services, often before they have rules for it.

The stakes are already visible. In September 2020, Amsterdam and Helsinki launched public registers of the algorithms and AI systems they use. In Toronto, residents and advocates objected to the data collection Sidewalk Labs planned for Quayside, and the project was cancelled in May 2020, citing the economic effects of COVID-19.

My senior thesis, which placed 3rd at the UC San Diego Urban Expo, looked at this through three lenses: governance, transparency and inclusion. It asked how cities are integrating AI into planning practice, and who decides, who can see how a system works and whose needs shape the design.

Role
Student researcher, UC San Diego Urban Studies & Planning
When
Senior thesis · UC San Diego Urban Expo
Status
Completed (senior thesis poster)
Methods
Practitioner interviews, Review of commercial AI and machine-learning platforms, Spatial analysis, Policy research
Tools and data
ArcGIS StoryMaps, GIS

Who decides, who sees, who counts: the question

Cities are starting to use artificial intelligence and machine learning in planning and public services, often before they have rules for it. My senior thesis, Defining A.I. Urban Dynamics: The Role of A.I. Urban Intelligence, asked how cities are integrating AI into planning practice.

I looked at that question through three lenses that recur in smart-city debates. Governance asks who decides. Transparency asks who can see how a system works. Inclusion asks whose needs shape the design.

Those lenses connect to the theme that runs through all of my work: who gets what in cities. An algorithm that routes inspections, ranks requests or flags risk is a decision about how public attention and resources are allocated. This project is the starting point for my GeoAI for Cities series.

Disrupted, not dismantled: the research behind it

The thesis sits in a body of work that treats the smart city as a governance question as much as a technical one. Three sources frame it well.

  • Michael Batty (2018), in an editorial for Environment and Planning B, argues that urban planning and design will be disrupted but not dismantled by AI, and that the field has to work these capabilities into its own methods rather than resist them. That is the practitioner-facing question this thesis picks up.
  • Rob Kitchin (2014), in GeoJournal, examines the real-time city built on streams of urban data. He weighs promised gains in efficiency and transparency against concerns that include surveillance, corporate control of city systems and technical vulnerability. Those concerns map onto the governance and transparency lenses I used.
  • UN-Habitat and Mila (2022), in AI and Cities: Risks, Applications and Governance, warn that using AI without governance mechanisms and attention to human rights can have negative, even catastrophic, effects. The report gives local governments practical recommendations, which makes it a useful checklist for the inclusion question.

Practitioners, platforms and maps: how I did it

My project record for this thesis is brief, so I describe the method only at the level it documents. The work combined three strands, and the result was presented as a poster.

  • Interviews with planning practitioners about how AI is entering their work.
  • A review of commercial AI and machine-learning platforms offered to cities.
  • Spatial analysis, presented as an ArcGIS StoryMap alongside the poster.

A framing that carried forward: what came out of it

The poster placed 3rd at the UC San Diego Urban Expo.

Its main contribution was a framing. It treats AI adoption in cities as a question of governance, transparency and inclusion, not only of technical capability, and it asks practitioners and vendors to answer to all three.

That framing carried forward. The GeoAI for Cities series continues the same line of questions about how spatial data and AI shape the distribution of public resources.

Toward algorithm registers: limits and next steps

This was an undergraduate thesis. The interviews and platform review describe practice at one moment, and they do not measure how AI tools changed outcomes for residents.

Since then, cities have built concrete transparency tools, such as public algorithm registers and review task forces. These make the question more testable. Next I would compare cities that publish algorithm registers with cities that do not, and ask whether disclosure changes which systems get adopted and who they affect.

Closer to home, I would inventory how agencies in the San Diego region disclose automated decision systems, and map which neighborhoods those systems touch most.

Case studies

  • Amsterdam, Netherlands and Helsinki, FinlandAlgorithm registers in Amsterdam and Helsinki

    In September 2020 both cities launched public registers of the algorithms and AI systems they use. Amsterdam's first entries included automated parking control, a holiday-rental fraud risk tool and a public-space issue reporting system, with each entry describing data used, human oversight and how discrimination is prevented.

    Lesson for this project: A register turns the transparency test into something a resident can actually check, entry by entry.

    Source
  • New York City, NYAutomated Decision Systems Task Force

    Local Law 49 of 2018 created a task force to recommend a process for reviewing the City's use of automated decision systems, with members from agencies, the private sector, nonprofits, advocates and researchers. It released its report on November 19, 2019.

    Lesson for this project: A city can legislate a review process for algorithms, and the task force model puts agencies and affected communities at the same table.

    Source
  • Toronto, Ontario, CanadaSidewalk Labs Quayside

    Sidewalk Labs cancelled its smart-city development on Toronto's Quayside waterfront in May 2020, citing the economic effects of COVID-19, after the site had been cut from 190 acres to 12. Residents and advocates had objected to the data collection the project planned.

    Lesson for this project: Public trust in how data will be governed shapes whether a smart-city project moves forward, alongside financing.

    Source

Sources
