Urban technology and policy · Research proposal · Urban Studies & Planning

Eyes in the Sky: Drones, AI, and Without Limitation

A research proposal and literature review on how drones paired with AI are changing practice on the ground, and what governance should guide this expanding aerial surveillance capability.

The drone that maps a crop can watch a street

Chula Vista Police Department launched its Drone as First Responder program on October 22, 2018. Its drones launch to 911 calls before officers arrive. Coverage of a 2023 ACLU report notes roughly 1,400 of 18,000 U.S. law enforcement agencies operating drones, some flying to minor calls.

Drones also do plainly useful work. After Hurricane Irma in September 2017, the FAA issued 132 airspace authorizations for drones to government agencies and critical infrastructure providers, which inspected roads, bridges, cell towers and power plants. A 2024 review of drone crop spraying reports that AI and precision systems cut pesticide use by up to 30 percent of the recommended dose in some cases.

This research proposal sets those uses side by side. No interviews, surveys or models have been completed yet. It asks how drone-AI technologies are providing novel views that transform practices on the ground, and what governance should guide them.

Role
Researcher and proposal author
When
Research proposal · Urban Studies & Planning
Status
Proposal
Methods
Literature review, Case studies (proposed): agriculture, disaster response, environmental monitoring, Geospatial modeling (proposed), Expert interviews (proposed), Public surveys (proposed)

Who flies, over whom: the question

Drones combined with AI and advanced imaging create new aerial views of human activity. This project asks: how are drone-AI technologies providing novel views that transform practices on the ground?

The question matters for cities because the same aircraft that maps crop stress or storm damage can also watch a street. Who flies, over whom, and under what rules is a question of who gets protection and who gets watched.

The goal is policy-facing. By setting out opportunities and risks side by side, the work aims to inform governance strategies that steer these capabilities toward outcomes the public actually benefits from.

FAA rules, ACLU limits and crop spraying: the research behind it

The proposal builds on regulation, civil liberties research and applied studies. These are the anchors I would point a reader to first.

  • FAA Part 107 governs commercial flights of small drones under 55 pounds. Pilots need a Remote Pilot Certificate, and flying beyond visual line of sight requires a waiver. That waiver process is where much of the expansion in public safety drone use happens.
  • The FAA Remote ID rule, published January 15, 2021, requires most registered drones to broadcast identification and location. Operators had to comply by September 16, 2023, and the FAA extended enforcement discretion to March 16, 2024. It makes drones visible to authorities, which raises the parallel question of what the public gets to see.
  • The ACLU report Eye-in-the-Sky Policing Needs Strict Limits (Jay Stanley, 2023) documents the spread of drone as first responder programs. Coverage of the report notes roughly 1,400 of 18,000 U.S. law enforcement agencies operating drones, and some programs flying to minor calls. It recommends limiting flights to serious emergencies and publishing flight data.
  • In agriculture, a 2024 review in the journal Drones (García-Munguía and colleagues) analyzed 100 studies of drone crop spraying. It reports that AI and precision systems cut pesticide use by up to 30 percent of the recommended dose in some cases, while noting the lack of standard testing protocols.

Three settings, five strands: how the study is designed

The project is at the proposal stage. Three documents exist: a literature review, a proposal subtitled Humanizing Drone-AI Innovation and Policy, and a data collection and management plan.

The proposal lays out a mixed-methods design. Each strand below is planned, not yet carried out, except the literature review.

  • Literature review synthesizing scholarship on aerial robotics and machine learning (completed as a draft document).
  • Case studies of drone-AI use in agriculture, disaster response and environmental monitoring.
  • Geospatial modeling to show where and how these applications operate.
  • Expert interviews to add practitioner knowledge to the academic literature.
  • Public surveys to measure attitudes toward increasing drone use.

A farm field is not a neighborhood: what exists so far

The deliverables to date are the literature review, the written proposal and the data plan. No interviews, surveys or models have been completed, so there are no findings to report yet.

What the design does establish is a structure for comparison. Putting agriculture, disaster response and environmental monitoring next to each other shows that the policy questions differ by setting. A farm field raises few privacy concerns, while a neighborhood flight raises many.

Narrowing to one setting: limits and next steps

The scope is broad. Three sectors, interviews, surveys and modeling are a lot for one study, and the rules keep moving as the FAA expands beyond-line-of-sight flying.

If I picked this up now, I would narrow it to one setting: police drone as first responder programs in San Diego County. Chula Vista publishes flight data, which would let me map where drones actually fly and compare that against neighborhood demographics and survey responses on trust.

Any survey or interview work would go through ethics review first, and the data plan would need clear rules for handling location data about residents.

Case studies

  • Chula Vista, CaliforniaDrone as First Responder program

    Chula Vista Police Department launched its Drone as First Responder program on October 22, 2018. Drones launch to 911 calls before officers arrive, under FAA beyond-visual-line-of-sight waivers granted in 2019 and expanded in 2021, and the department publishes flight data and bars recording private spaces without a warrant or emergency.

    Lesson for this project: Published flight logs make it possible to study where aerial attention actually lands, which is the governance question this project asks.

    Source
  • FloridaDrones after Hurricane Irma

    After Hurricane Irma in September 2017, the FAA issued 132 airspace authorizations for drones to government agencies and critical infrastructure providers. They inspected roads, bridges, cell towers and power plants and helped insurers survey damage.

    Lesson for this project: Disaster response shows the public benefit side of the ledger, and how fast airspace rules can flex in an emergency.

    Source

Urban technology and policy · USP Senior Sequence 186-187 · UC San Diego

Material Allocation in Urban Ecology

An early-stage proposal to map San Diego's flows of water, waste, building materials and food with GIS, and to ask which neighborhoods are served well by that infrastructure and which are not.

A recycling center has an address

A refill station, a recycling center or a food hub is a public good with a location. Some neighborhoods are closer to it than others. Cities take in water, energy, food and construction materials, and they send out waste. Where the facilities that handle those flows sit shapes daily life in every neighborhood.

San Diego has set targets for one of these flows. Its June 2015 Zero Waste Plan aims for 75 percent diversion by 2020, 90 percent by 2035 and zero waste by 2040. Its strategies include organics recycling infrastructure and a resource recovery park at Miramar Landfill. Those are sites, and sites can be mapped.

This is an early draft proposal, and no mapping has been carried out yet. It asks how GIS can map the current allocation of water, solid waste, construction materials and food in San Diego, and where those flows show spatial inefficiencies and inequities across neighborhoods.

Role
Student researcher (draft proposal)
When
USP Senior Sequence 186-187 · UC San Diego
Status
Proposal
Methods
Urban metabolism / material flow analysis (proposed), GIS mapping and spatial analysis (proposed), Network analysis for facility siting (proposed), Drone photogrammetry workflow (proposed)
Tools and data
City of San Diego Open Data Portal, SANDAG, SanGIS, CalRecycle waste characterization data, EPA WARM, USGS water use and land cover data, Pix4D or DroneDeploy (proposed)

Inputs, outputs and locations: the question

Cities take in huge amounts of water, energy, food and construction materials, and they send out waste. Where those flows go, and where the facilities that handle them sit, shapes daily life in every neighborhood.

This draft proposal asks how GIS can map the current allocation of key resource flows in San Diego, including water, solid waste, construction materials and food. It aims to find spatial inefficiencies and inequities in how those resources are distributed across neighborhoods.

That makes it a who-gets-what question. A refill station, a recycling center or a food hub is a public good with a location, and some neighborhoods are closer to it than others.

Cities as organisms: the research behind it

The proposal draws on urban metabolism research, which treats a city like an organism with inputs, stocks and outputs. The points below ground it and set honest expectations about the data.

  • Kennedy, Cuddihy and Engel-Yan (2007), in the Journal of Industrial Ecology, compared the metabolism of eight metropolitan regions on five continents. Most showed rising per-capita use of water, energy and materials. They also note that full metabolism data exist for few cities, and call for standard measurement conventions.
  • EPA's Waste Reduction Model (WARM) compares greenhouse gas emissions, energy savings and economic impacts across source reduction, recycling, composting, anaerobic digestion, combustion and landfilling. It is the tool the proposal names for estimating the climate benefit of different strategies.
  • CalRecycle's waste characterization data break disposal down by business group and material for every California jurisdiction. CalRecycle cautions that local figures are estimates built from statewide study averages and local employment and population, not samples taken in each city.
  • USGS publishes water use estimates by category at state and county level, with monthly estimates at the watershed scale for 2000 to 2020. That resolution is coarser than the neighborhood scale this proposal targets.

Flows, networks and drone imagery: how the study would work

The proposal outlines a GIS-based material flow analysis for San Diego. Every step below is planned.

Most of the named data sources exist and are public. The City of San Diego Open Data Portal offers downloadable datasets across city departments. SANDAG provides socioeconomic estimates, forecasts and transportation modeling. SanGIS publishes regional layers such as address points linked to parcel numbers, roads, rights-of-way and transit stops.

  • Map current flows of water, solid waste, construction materials and food, and compare them across neighborhoods.
  • Join flows to population density, zoning, transportation networks, socioeconomic data and built infrastructure.
  • Use network analysis to test better locations for water refill stations, waste transfer stations, local food hubs and recycling centers.
  • Collect site imagery with drones: set ground control points, plan overlapping flight grids, process images into georeferenced orthomosaics and 3D models, then digitize buildings, roads and facilities.
  • Share results through interactive maps and 3D views for planners and sustainability managers.

An outline, not a study: what the draft produced

This is an early outline, not a completed study. It produced a research statement, an inventory of candidate data sources, a step-by-step drone mapping workflow and a list of possible comparison cities.

The comparison list includes Copenhagen, Amsterdam, Curitiba, Tokyo, Austin, London, Singapore and Masdar City. No mapping, network analysis or flights have been carried out.

Four studies, not one: limits and next steps

The biggest limit is data resolution. CalRecycle jurisdiction figures are modeled rather than sampled, and USGS water use is reported at county or watershed level, so neighborhood-scale flows would rely on proxies such as parcels, land use and service routes.

The scope is also too wide. Water, waste, construction materials and food are four studies, not one, and I would also need to confirm which waste collection data the City actually publishes.

Next I would start with one flow, solid waste and organics, and tie it to San Diego's Zero Waste Plan. I would map where diversion facilities sit relative to the neighborhoods they serve, then add equity measures from SANDAG data.

Case studies

  • Amsterdam, NetherlandsAmsterdam Circular Strategy 2020-2025

    Amsterdam's strategy aims to halve the use of primary raw materials by 2030 and become fully circular by 2050. It uses the doughnut model and focuses on three value chains: food and organic waste, consumer goods, and the built environment, with a monitor to track ecological and social impact.

    Lesson for this project: Organizing by value chain and pairing it with a monitor is a workable way to narrow a city-wide material flow study.

    Source
  • London, United KingdomLondon's Circular Economy Route Map

    In June 2017 the London Waste and Recycling Board published a route map covering the built environment, food, textiles, electricals and plastics. It set out more than 100 actions and estimated net benefits of at least 7 billion pounds a year across those sectors by 2036.

    Lesson for this project: A sector-by-sector plan with named actions shows how flow analysis can turn into specific decisions for a city.

    Source
  • San Diego, CaliforniaCity of San Diego Zero Waste Plan

    San Diego's June 2015 Zero Waste Plan targets 75 percent diversion by 2020, 90 percent by 2035 and zero waste by 2040. Strategies include organics recycling infrastructure, minimum diversion requirements for franchise haulers and a resource recovery park at Miramar Landfill.

    Lesson for this project: The plan's facilities and targets give this project a local policy hook and a concrete set of sites to map.

    Source

Reimagining La Jolla Village Square

A site analysis and redesign proposal that reconnects a car-oriented shopping center to the new UC San Diego Blue Line trolley with a direct pathway, a split building and a central open space.

A trolley stop beside a parking lot

On November 21, 2021, the UC San Diego Blue Line extension opened 11 miles of light rail and nine stations. One of them, Nobel Drive, sits on the western side of La Jolla Village Square.

The center already has a lot. Ralph's and Trader Joe's for groceries. Best Buy, Marshalls and PetSmart. Club Pilates and La Jolla Fencing Academy. About ten food tenants, mostly chains. But the whole site is built around parking, and it is laid out for one kind of trip: drive in for one errand, then leave.

The station is already next door. The missing piece is a clear, pleasant walk from the platform into the center. This proposal asks how the site could be reorganized so people arrive on foot and by transit, linger, and support local businesses.

Role
Designer and author
When
UC San Diego · Design proposal
Status
Proposal
Methods
Site analysis, Tenant and land use inventory, Site diagramming, Implementation planning
Tools and data
Site diagrams

Built for cars, next to a trolley: the question

La Jolla Village Square is a large shopping center with groceries, big-box stores, restaurants and gyms. It is built around parking, yet it now sits next to a trolley station.

I asked how the site could be reorganized so people arrive on foot and by transit, linger, and support local businesses, instead of driving in for one errand and leaving.

The goal was a site diagram and analysis that a property owner, the city and the community could react to.

Lessons from retrofitted malls: the research behind it

Two bodies of work shaped the proposal.

  • Retrofitting suburbia. Ellen Dunham-Jones and June Williamson document how dead or dying malls and strip centers have been rebuilt as walkable, mixed-use places, and also how some fall short, staying cut off by wide arterials or priced out of reach of the people who work there.
  • Built environment and travel. Ewing and Cervero's 2010 meta-analysis found walking responds most to land use mix, intersection density and nearby destinations, and transit use to proximity to transit and street network design. That is the case for a direct, legible path from the station into the center.

From Ralph's to the fencing academy: how I read the site

I started with an inventory of the existing tenants and uses. The center holds grocery anchors (Ralph's, Trader Joe's, Cost Plus World Market), large stores such as Best Buy, Marshalls, Ross and PetSmart, fitness and recreation tenants such as Club Pilates, YogaSIX and La Jolla Fencing Academy, and about ten food tenants, mostly chains.

I then looked at land use, circulation, public space and architecture, and drew site diagrams for the proposed changes. The plan sets out objectives, design moves, challenges and an implementation sequence.

A path, a split and a plaza: the proposal

The core idea is to bring in local eateries and shops alongside the existing chains, and to make the center a place you can walk through and explore.

Each design move is a proposal, not a built project.

  • Direct pathway to transit: a straight, clear walking route from the center to the trolley area, to ease pedestrian flow and reduce reliance on cars.
  • Building split: divide the existing building into two sections, opening a central space for gatherings, events, arts and dining.
  • Roundabout: a roundabout at the central entry to smooth traffic, mark the entrance and calm vehicle speeds near pedestrians.
  • Community elements: public art, green space, pedestrian paths and gathering areas, with sustainable design and stormwater management.
  • Implementation: feasibility study, detailed design with architects and landscape designers, engagement with residents, businesses and transit authorities, phased construction, and public communication.

Untested ideas and a roundabout problem: limits and next steps

This is a concept. I have not tested traffic flows, costs, leases or zoning, and the stakeholder engagement in the objectives has not yet happened.

The roundabout and the pedestrian core pull in different directions. Placing vehicle circulation in the center of the open space could undercut the walkable heart the building split is meant to create.

Next, I would count pedestrians between the station and the center, map walking routes and crossings, and talk with tenants and nearby residents. I would also test a version that keeps cars at the edge and puts the plaza between the station and the stores.

Case studies

  • La Jolla Village, San Diego, CANobel Drive trolley station

    The UC San Diego Blue Line extension added 11 miles of light rail and nine stations, opening on November 21, 2021. Nobel Drive station sits on the western side of La Jolla Village Square and is reached from the center's northern entrance.

    Lesson for this project: The station is already next door, so the missing piece is a clear, pleasant walk from the platform into the center.

    Source
  • Mashpee, MAMashpee Commons

    A failed 1960s strip shopping plaza was master-planned from 1988 into a traditional town center with continuous street frontage, local and national retail, and planned housing including affordable and senior units.

    Lesson for this project: A strip center can become a town center over time if streets and storefronts, not parking, organize the site.

    Source
  • Lakewood, COBelmar (former Villa Italia Mall)

    A dead regional mall was replaced with a walkable mixed-use district with a public plaza and restaurant patios, praised by Dunham-Jones as a retrofit success. A later assessment found it still walled off by six-lane avenues and unaffordable for its own retail workers.

    Lesson for this project: Good internal design is not enough; the edges and the trolley link decide whether a retrofit serves the surrounding community.

    Source

CurbCall: Resident-Ranked Infrastructure Repairs for San Diego

A phone-first prototype where San Diego residents photograph a broken sidewalk, pothole or dark street, tick a short checklist, and vote on what each part of the city should fix first.

85,000 open cases and no way to say what matters most

In March 2026, San Diego's Get It Done app had about 85,000 open cases. A 72-hour parking complaint took about 14 days to close in Pacific Beach. In Del Mar Mesa, Torrey Highlands and Carmel Mountain, it took about 125.

Get It Done works like a complaint inbox. One report becomes one ticket. It can count complaints, but it cannot show what residents think matters most, or which neighborhoods are being heard. Research on 311 complaints in Kansas City found that low-income and minority neighborhoods were less likely to report street problems, despite greater measured need. Rank repairs by complaint volume, and that gap becomes a service gap.

CurbCall is my answer in prototype form. Residents photograph a broken sidewalk, pothole or dark street and vote on what each part of the city should fix first. It has not been tested with residents yet. It is built to ask one question: if residents can report and vote on what to fix first, whose problems get heard, and does that match where the city responds?

Role
Product lead: concept, feature design, user flow and research framing
When
2026 · Working prototype
Status
Prototype · not yet tested with residents
Methods
Product and user-flow design, Equity-aware ranking design (per-area rankings), Spatial database design, Planned comparison with Get It Done response times
Tools and data
Web app with shared database, PostgreSQL/PostGIS (design), Web mapping
Open the prototypeCode & database on GitHub

An inbox that counts complaints but not priorities

If residents can report and vote on what to fix first, whose problems get heard, and does that match where the city responds? CurbCall is the product side of my research theme, who gets what in cities.

San Diego's own reporting app, Get It Done, works like a complaint inbox: one report becomes one ticket. In March 2026 it had nearly 85,000 open cases, and closure times varied widely by neighborhood. An inbox can count complaints, but it cannot show what residents think matters most, why, or which neighborhoods are being heard.

What 311 research warns about reporting tools

Three lines of research shaped the design. Each one points to a specific risk that a reporting tool has to plan for.

  • Bias in 311 data. Kontokosta and Hong (2021, Sustainable Cities and Society) studied complaints in Kansas City and found that low-income and minority neighborhoods were less likely to report street condition or nuisance issues, despite greater measured need. If a city ranks repairs by complaint volume, that gap becomes a service gap. This is why CurbCall ranks within areas rather than only citywide.
  • Coproduction and the digital divide. Clark, Brudney and Jang (2013, Public Administration Review) treat 311 reporting as citizens coproducing public services. In Boston they found lower-income neighborhoods used 311 less overall, though smartphone requests were more evenly spread. This is why I designed for phones first and planned ways to take part without a smartphone.
  • Participatory budgeting. New York City Council's participatory budgeting has let residents vote directly on capital projects since 2011. It shows that residents can rank public spending, and that turnout and language access decide whose priorities count.

Snap it, vote it, see the ranking

CurbCall is a working web prototype covering all of San Diego, with 124 neighborhoods grouped into 7 areas. It follows three steps.

  • Snap it. Take a photo, drop a pin, pick a category and tick a short infrastructure checklist.
  • Vote it. Swipe right to fix it, left if it can wait, and give a reason: safety, accessibility, kids and schools, flooding, or heat.
  • See the ranking. A city view ranks reports by net support within each of seven areas, from North to South Bay, so busy neighborhoods do not drown out quieter ones.

Five design choices against complaint-driven bias

Most of the work was deciding what the tool should and should not allow. Each choice responds to a known weakness in complaint-driven systems.

  • A required photo and a short checklist, so every report is comparable rather than free text.
  • One vote per person per report, with reasons, so city staff see the why as well as the count.
  • Rankings per area, not just citywide, so neighborhoods that report less are not ranked last by default.
  • A light, familiar look modeled on apps people already use, so it does not feel like a government form.
  • Planned support for Spanish, Tagalog and Vietnamese, and ways to take part without a smartphone.

A working prototype with no real users yet

The prototype works end to end, but it has no real users yet. The 17 reports in the app are labeled examples for demonstration, so nothing here is a finding about San Diego residents.

The research value comes next. Paired with Get It Done response times, CurbCall could show where residents are waiting longest and whose voices the city hears.

The database is designed around PostgreSQL and PostGIS, so every report carries a location that can be joined to neighborhoods, areas and city service records. That spatial structure is what would let the tool compare what residents rank first with what the city actually closes first.

The comparison I want to make is simple to state. If the neighborhoods that vote most urgently for a repair are also the ones waiting longest under Get It Done, that is evidence the current inbox is not hearing them.

Built with an AI assistant from my product direction

The app, database and repository were built with an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) from my product direction across several design rounds. I set the concept, features, user flow and research framing.

Where resident voting can go wrong, and what comes next

Voting tools can repeat the bias they are meant to fix. People with more time, better connectivity and more trust in government will vote more, and per-area rankings soften that but do not remove it.

A required photo also raises the bar to take part. It makes reports comparable, but it may exclude people without a camera phone, which is why the planned non-smartphone options matter.

A ranking is also not a budget. Residents can say what matters, but the city still decides what it can afford and what is legally required, so the tool should inform repair decisions rather than set them.

Next, I plan to pilot with community partners in Southeast San Diego, Mid-City and South Bay, write consent language and complete an ethics (IRB) check before collecting any research data, and add before-and-after photos with progress tracking from Reported to Fixed.

Case studies

  • San Diego, CAGet It Done backlog

    The city's service request app had about 85,000 open cases in March 2026. Hoodline reported 72-hour parking complaints taking about 14 days to close in Pacific Beach but about 125 days in Del Mar Mesa, Torrey Highlands and Carmel Mountain, with hundreds pending in Southeastern San Diego, Skyline-Paradise Hills and Encanto.

    Lesson for this project: An inbox records demand but not priority, and response times differ by neighborhood, which is the gap CurbCall is designed to make visible.

    Source
  • United Kingdom (also deployed abroad)FixMyStreet

    Run by the UK charity mySociety (under that name since 2007), FixMyStreet maps reports of potholes, broken lights and similar problems and sends them to the responsible council, and its open-source platform is used in places such as Zurich and Sweden.

    Lesson for this project: Public, mapped reports and open code show that a reporting tool can be transparent and portable, which CurbCall should match.

    Source
  • New York City, NYNYC Participatory Budgeting

    Since 2011, residents aged 11 and up have voted on capital projects in participating Council districts. In the FY 2027 cycle, nearly 130,000 people in 22 districts allocated almost $25 million, with ballots in 12 languages and over 100 in-person sites.

    Lesson for this project: Resident voting gains legitimacy when it is tied to real money and reaches people through many languages and in-person options.

    Source

GeoAI for Cities: Research Series and Website

A research website and article series on GeoAI and urban decision-making: an academic primer, an exploratory Manhattan case study, and original studies to come.

When a ranking gets called AI

Picture two tools that rank the same neighborhoods with the same data. One is a rule a planner wrote by hand. The other is called AI. The second can sound more objective, even though the ranking is the same.

That is the risk of a term everyone uses differently. Vendors, labs and city agencies apply GeoAI to everything from detecting buildings in satellite images to ranking neighborhoods for services. And the ranking rule is not a detail.

This series defines GeoAI carefully, traces how cities used spatial technology long before the term existed, and keeps returning to one question. When cities use these tools to rank and decide, who benefits?

Role
Author and editor: topics, framing and research direction
When
2026 · Ongoing
Status
Ongoing
Methods
Literature and history review, Exploratory case study, Original spatial analysis, Interactive web mapping, Science communication
Tools and data
Research website, Interactive maps and figures
Browse the seriesManhattan, MeasuredWebsite sourceShared database

Why GeoAI needs a careful definition

GeoAI is a popular term with a vague meaning. Vendors, labs and city agencies use it for very different things, from detecting buildings in satellite images to ranking neighborhoods for services.

That vagueness matters for cities. When a tool is called AI, it can sound more objective than a rule a planner wrote by hand, even when it is ranking the same places with the same data.

I wanted a public body of work that does three things: defines GeoAI carefully, shows how spatial technology was used in cities long before the term existed, and asks the question I care most about. When cities use these tools to rank and decide, who benefits?

From Goodchild to Local Law 49

The series draws on two academic traditions and one policy debate. Together they frame GeoAI as a continuation of GIScience with new stakes for city governance.

  • GIScience. Michael Goodchild's 1992 paper in the International Journal of Geographical Information Systems argued that GIS needed to become a science, not only a system, with spatial analysis at its core. The series treats GeoAI as the latest chapter in that argument rather than a clean break.
  • Defining GeoAI. Janowicz, Gao, McKenzie, Hu and Bhaduri (2020, IJGIS) describe GeoAI as spatially explicit artificial intelligence and ask whether it only applies general AI or contributes something distinct. Industry definitions, such as Esri's description of AI fused with geospatial data, science and technology, are broader. Part 1 sets these side by side.
  • Algorithmic accountability in cities. New York City's Automated Decision Systems Task Force, created by Local Law 49 of 2018, recommended that agencies report on high-priority systems and assess them for disproportionate impacts. That framing, that a ranking system is a public decision, runs through every part of the series.

A primer, a Manhattan case study and an original study

The series currently has three pieces, each written for a general reader without dropping the rigor an academic reader expects.

  • Part 1: What Is GeoAI? An academic-style primer with definitions, tables, a timeline of GIS and spatial technology, and paths for both industry practitioners and academics.
  • Manhattan, Measured. An exploratory case study, with case studies and timelines of how researchers measured the city before and after machine learning.

History first, one question throughout

I chose the topics, set the framing, and decided which questions each piece had to answer. I rejected drafts that felt generic, because the point of the series is to say something specific about cities rather than to summarize the field.

The history matters as much as the methods. Cities were mapping need, risk and service long before machine learning, and many of the equity questions people now ask about AI were already present in older tools like overlay maps and indicator rankings.

Each piece connects back to one question: who gets what in cities. The primer defines the tools, the Manhattan piece shows how measurement has changed, and the shade study tests what happens when a ranking rule decides who benefits.

Writing, figures and the website were drafted with an AI assistant (Claude, Anthropic) under my editorial direction. Background articles are being fact-checked against sources before formal citation.

From a definition to an original finding

The series is a working research identity rather than a finished product. It shows I can explain technical ideas to a general audience without losing rigor, and that I can move from a definition to an original study built on public data.

It also showed that a heat-illness model which looked useful on random test splits did worse than guessing the average when asked to predict a borough it had not seen. That is a concrete warning for any city that wants to borrow a model trained somewhere else.

Drafts, not yet peer reviewed, and what comes next

The background articles are not yet fully fact-checked or formally cited, and nothing in the series is peer reviewed. Until that work is done, readers should treat the primer and the Manhattan piece as drafts.

Next, I plan to fact-check and cite all background articles, add a research statement page and a disclosure note in the site footer, and publish Part 3.

Case studies

  • New York City, NYAutomated Decision Systems Task Force

    Local Law 49 of 2018 created a task force to recommend how the city should review its automated decision systems. Its November 2019 report called for a central management function, public education, agency reporting on high-priority systems, and checks for disproportionate impacts, and it openly recorded disagreement about how much authority oversight should have.

    Lesson for this project: Defining which systems count and who reviews them is the hard part, so the series should be precise about which spatial tools it calls GeoAI.

    Source
  • Amsterdam, Netherlands and Helsinki, FinlandPublic algorithm registers

    In September 2020 both cities launched public registers explaining the algorithms they use. Amsterdam's listed automated parking control, holiday-rental fraud risk assessment and a public-space issue reporting system; Helsinki's listed service chatbots and a library book recommender.

    Lesson for this project: A plain-language public register is a practical model for the disclosure a city should give residents about spatial ranking tools.

    Source

GeoAI for Cities, Part 1, October 2026

What Is GeoAI? Definitions, Foundations and Five Verbs Across U.S. Cities

GeoAI is artificial intelligence that uses location as part of how it works. In this part I define the term from the research literature, trace where it came from, explain what makes an AI method spatial, and then check one documented U.S. city example for each of the five verbs against its source.

By Johan Fernandez. About a 30-minute read, with 42 sources.

Abstract

This part covers the basics. It looks at how the literature defines GeoAI, its history from 1970 to today, the principles and four tests that make AI spatial, the GIS it grew out of, and its building blocks. Then it walks through five verbs for what GeoAI does in cities (see, find, measure, predict and decide), each with a documented example, and ends with practical paths for city teams and for academics.

Key findings

  • Definitions differ in emphasis, but the research ones agree that location has to be part of how the model reasons.
  • AI in geography has been discussed since at least 1984; a dedicated GeoAI workshop at ACM SIGSPATIAL began in 2017.
  • A 2022 review of 581 urban geography papers found the field still early, with spatially explicit models underdeveloped.
  • In U.S. cities, detection has the strongest reported results (97% for potholes in San José). Deciding where money goes has the least evidence behind it.

On this page

1. Defining GeoAI 2. Where the term comes from 3. GIS and spatial technology 4. What makes AI spatial 5. Four tests for GeoAI 6. Building blocks 7. GeoAI, GIS and other AI 8. Five verbs in U.S. cities 9. Evidence at a glance 10. Paths for practitioners and academics 11. Limits and risks Sources and citation

A lot of city work comes down to choosing a location: which street to repave, which drain to inspect, which hillside to protect before fire season.

Most cities respond after something has already happened, like a 311 call, a flood or a 911 call. GeoAI uses data that cities already collect to predict where problems are forming, so crews can get there sooner.

1. Defining GeoAI

GeoAI is short for geospatial artificial intelligence. The definitions vary, but most describe machine learning applied to data with locations attached, and ask what changes when location becomes part of the reasoning. I compare six of them below.

Table 1. How the literature defines GeoAI. Wording is quoted where marked, otherwise paraphrased.

SourceFieldDefinitionEmphasis
VoPham et al., 201814Environmental epidemiologyCombines spatial science, machine learning (including deep learning), data mining and high-performance computing to extract knowledge from spatial big data.Methods and computing
Janowicz et al., 20201GIScience“A subfield of spatial data science” that uses advances in techniques and data cultures to support more intelligent geographic information, methods, systems and services.Spatial explicitness
Li, 202015GIScience“An emergent spatial analytical framework for data-intensive GIScience,” using machine learning and advanced computing to analyze geospatial big data through data-driven and knowledge-driven methods.Big data and scale
Hu et al., 201916Computer science (ACM SIGSPATIAL)An interdisciplinary field that brings machine learning and deep learning to geographic problems.Interdisciplinarity
Gao, 202117Geography reference workThe integration of geospatial studies and AI, especially machine learning and deep learning, to build programs that mimic human perception, spatial reasoning and discovery about geographic phenomena.Reasoning like a geographer
Esri2IndustryAI combined with geospatial data to understand opportunity, environmental impact and operational risk.Business value

The research definitions share one requirement: location has to do some work inside the model. If you predict a road’s condition from its age and traffic, that’s ordinary machine learning. If the model also uses the fact that the road sits below a failing culvert, under trees whose roots lift the pavement, that’s GeoAI.

Working definition used in this series. GeoAI is AI whose reasoning depends on location. A method counts if it passes at least one of the four tests in Table 4.

2. Where the term comes from

The idea is older than the name. Geographers were already trying AI on spatial problems in the 1980s. In the 2010s came methods that learn from images, along with enough data to train them. The main milestones are in Table 2.

Table 2. Milestones in the lineage of GeoAI.

YearMilestoneWhy it matters
1970Tobler states the “first law of geography”: everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things.18The principle of spatial dependence that GeoAI models must respect.
1984Smith asks how artificial intelligence applies to geographical problem solving.19One of the first sustained treatments of AI in geography.
1986Couclelis sets out conjectures on what AI could become in geography.20Treats AI as a way to represent geographic knowledge as well as compute with it.
1997Openshaw and Openshaw publish Artificial Intelligence in Geography.21Brings neural networks, expert systems, genetic algorithms and fuzzy logic into one geographic toolkit.
2015LeCun, Bengio and Hinton review the rise of deep learning.22Convolutional networks make large-scale image analysis, including satellite and street imagery, practical.
2016Jean et al. combine satellite imagery and machine learning to estimate poverty in five African countries.23A widely cited study showing that imagery can measure economic conditions where surveys are thin.
2017The first GeoAI workshop is held at ACM SIGSPATIAL in Los Angeles, accepting 8 of 14 submissions.16GeoAI becomes a named research community; the workshop grew to 17 papers by 2019.
2020Janowicz et al. edit an IJGIS special issue on spatially explicit AI.1Source of the four tests for spatial explicitness used in this part.
2022Liu and Biljecki review 581 papers on spatially explicit GeoAI in urban geography.24Finds the field still early, with spatially explicit models in need of development.
2023NASA and IBM release Prithvi, a geospatial foundation model trained on satellite imagery.25,7One pre-trained model adapted to tasks such as flood and burn-scar mapping.
2024Mai et al. test foundation models on geographic tasks.26Large language models do well on place-name text tasks but trail task-specific models when images and map data are combined.

So GeoAI has two roots. One is the series of AI methods that geographers have tried on spatial problems over the decades. The other is Tobler’s older rule that nearby things are more related.

3. The GIS and spatial technology behind GeoAI

GeoAI builds on about six decades of spatial technology. The first GIS was built in Canada from 1962 to 1968 under Roger Tomlinson.37 Howard Fisher founded the Harvard Laboratory for Computer Graphics in 1965, Esri followed in 1969, and ARC/INFO, the first commercial GIS, in 1981.38

Location data became much easier to get after a few changes. Landsat 1 launched in 1972, and the USGS made its archive free in 2008.39 In May 2000 the U.S. ended deliberate GPS degradation, giving civilians 10 to 20 meters or better.40 Starting in 2004, OpenStreetMap let volunteers build an open map.41 Figure 2 places these alongside the history of AI in geography.

GeoAI sits near the top of a stack of technologies (Figure 3), so errors in any layer below it carry up into its results.

4. What makes AI spatial

Geographic data break one of the basic assumptions in machine learning, that observations are independent of each other. Four principles follow from this, listed in Table 3.

Table 3. Four spatial principles that distinguish geographic data, and what each means for an AI model.

PrincipleStatementConsequence for AICity example
Spatial dependence18Nearby observations tend to be similar.Random train and test splits put neighbors on both sides, which inflates accuracy. Spatial cross-validation holds out whole areas instead.30Pavement on one block predicts pavement on the next, so a model can look accurate just by memorizing neighborhoods.
Spatial heterogeneity27The same relationship can differ from place to place.A model trained in one city may not transfer to another. Methods such as geographically weighted regression let relationships vary across space.31House age may predict lead pipes in one city and not in another with a different building history.
Scale and zoning (the modifiable areal unit problem)28Results change with the size and shape of the units used.Aggregating to blocks, tracts or districts can change a model's answer, so the choice of unit needs a stated reason.A neighborhood can look well served at the tract level and underserved at the block-group level.
Local association29Citywide averages can hide local clusters.Local statistics find hot spots that global measures miss, and make useful model inputs.An average flood rate hides a cluster of intersections that flood every storm.

Goodchild and Li argue that, because of this, a finding from one place can inform work in another place but can’t settle the question there.27 In the same way, a model’s accuracy figure describes the area where it was tested.

5. Four tests for GeoAI

Janowicz and colleagues, building on Goodchild, propose four tests for whether a model is spatially explicit. A model only has to pass one of them.1 Below, each test has a city example of a model that passes and one that doesn’t.

Table 4. Four tests for spatially explicit models (Janowicz et al., 2020, after Goodchild), with city examples.

TestA model passes when…PassesDoes not pass
InvarianceIts results change if the same things are moved somewhere else.A flood-risk score that depends on elevation and the impervious area upstream.A pipe-failure score based only on pipe age and material; moving the pipe changes nothing.
RepresentationLocations, spatial relations or place names appear in the model itself.A model that uses distance to the nearest storm drain as an input.A table where the address is only a record ID.
FormulationSpatial concepts such as neighborhood are built into how it computes.A parcel score that includes its neighbors' scores, as in a spatial lag or graph model.Each parcel scored in isolation.
OutcomeThe spatial form of its output differs from its input.Point sensor readings turned into a continuous risk surface, or calls turned into a ranked street network.Points in, the same points out with a label.

If a vendor is pitching “AI-powered GIS” to a city, one useful question is which of these tests it passes. If it passes none, it’s ordinary analytics with a map attached, and its accuracy claims should be read with the principles in Table 3 in mind.

6. Building blocks

GeoAI systems tend to be built from the same layers, shown in Figure 1. After it, Table 5 covers the main data sources and Table 6 the method families.

Table 5. Main data sources for urban GeoAI.

DataWhat it capturesTypical sourceExample in research or practiceCaution
Satellite and aerial imageryLand cover, roofs, impervious surface, vegetation, change over timeLandsat, Sentinel-2, aerial surveysPoverty estimation23; Prithvi flood and burn-scar mapping25Cloud cover, revisit time and resolution limit what can be seen.
Street-level imageryFacades, sidewalks, signs, vehicles, road surfaceStreet View, cameras on city vehiclesNeighborhood demographics from cars33; San José road pilot4; a review of street-view research34Covers drivable streets more than alleys and paths; privacy.
Elevation and LiDARTerrain, slopes, flow paths, building heightsLidar surveys, digital elevation modelsDrainage and flood-path modelingCostly to collect and often years out of date.
SensorsRainfall, flow, air quality, traffic countsCity and utility sensor networksStormwater and traffic monitoringSparse and gappy; sensors fail where conditions are worst.
Administrative recordsParcels, permits, work orders, inspections, 311 callsCity systemsFlint lead-pipe model36; Chicago food inspections11Records show where the city looked, which may differ from where the problems are.12
Census and surveysIncome, housing, populationAmerican Community SurveyForecasting neighborhood change6Large margins of error at small geographies.
Text with place names311 descriptions, reports, news, social mediaCity and public textPlace-name recognition, where language models perform well26Ambiguous names; models can invent locations.

Table 6. Method families used in GeoAI, and how each handles space.

MethodHow it uses spaceCity exampleReference
Convolutional neural networksLearn patterns from neighboring pixels in imagesDetecting potholes, smoke and roof typesLeCun et al., 201522
Local spatial statisticsMeasure whether each place resembles its neighborsFinding clusters of repeat flooding or complaintsAnselin, 199529
Geographically weighted regressionLets relationships vary from place to placeShowing that drivers of runoff differ by neighborhoodFotheringham et al., 200231
Tree ensembles with spatial featuresAdd distances, neighbor averages and location as inputsForecasting neighborhood changeReades et al., 201935; Gilling et al., 20216
Graph neural networksTreat roads, pipes or parcels as connected nodesModeling a pipe or street network as a wholeKipf and Welling, 201732
Spatial cross-validationTests a model on whole areas it has not seenChecking a model trained on one district works in anotherRoberts et al., 201730
Geospatial foundation modelsPre-train once on broad imagery, then fine-tuneFlood and burn-scar mappingJakubik et al., 202325; Mai et al., 202426

Most cities already have much of the data they would need. The harder part is representing it spatially inside a model. For small teams, older spatial statistics often work better than foundation models, and a cluster analysis is quick to run.

7. GeoAI, GIS and other AI

GeoAI overlaps with GIS, conventional machine learning and generative AI. The main difference is how each one treats location (Table 7). Generative AI gets the most attention of the four, but it mostly handles location as words and can misplace or invent places.

Table 7. GeoAI compared with GIS, conventional machine learning and generative AI.

ApproachMain jobHow it treats locationTypical outputExample question
GISStore, map, query and analyze spatial dataAs geometry and layersMaps, overlays, measurementsWhich parcels sit in the 100-year floodplain?
Conventional machine learningPredict from attributesAs one more column, or not at allA score per recordWhich pipes are oldest and most likely to fail?
GeoAILearn from spatial data with spatial structure in the modelAs part of the reasoning: neighbors, distance, imageryRanked maps, detections, risk surfacesWhich blocks are likely to flood in the next storm, given what drains into them?
Generative AIGenerate text or imagesMostly as wordsText, summaries, imagesSummarize these 311 complaints by neighborhood. (Can misplace or invent locations.26)
Spatially explicit
A model whose results change when you move things to a different location, even if nothing else about them changes.
Foundation model
A large model pre-trained once on broad data, such as satellite imagery, then adapted to specific tasks.
Spatial cross-validation
Testing a model on whole areas left out of training, so nearby look-alikes cannot inflate its accuracy.
CIP
Capital Improvement Plan: a city's multi-year list of funded infrastructure projects.
MS4
Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System, the stormwater permit program cities report under.

Key terms used in this part.

8. Five verbs in U.S. cities

I group what GeoAI does in cities into five verbs: see (detect in imagery), find (locate problems), measure (score condition), predict (forecast problems) and decide (rank where resources go). The map tour has seven examples that cover all five.

As you scroll through the tour, the map moves to each place.

Tour map (WGS84)
Drag to pan, use Ctrl+scroll or pinch to zoom, and click a pin for details
Seven examples across the United States
The map could not load. Every location is named in the text.
United States

Seven examples of the five verbs

Each pin is a documented example, and each color is a verb. There are seven examples: six places in California, Indiana, Illinois, New York and Michigan, plus a nationwide census-tract study.

La Jolla, California (statewide camera network)

See: spotting fires before a 911 call

ALERTCalifornia uses AI on mountaintop cameras to look for smoke. In 2024 it detected 1,668 fires, and for 636 of them (about 38%) the detection came before any dispatch record.3

San José, California

Find: locating potholes without waiting for a 311 call

Cameras mounted on city vehicles identified potholes with 97% accuracy and debris with 88%. City staff checked the detections against the footage.4

West Lafayette, Indiana (surveys in five states)

Measure: rating roads from ordinary cars

PaveX rates pavement using low-cost sensors on ordinary vehicles. Since January 2025 it has surveyed more than 6,200 miles in Indiana, Michigan, North Carolina, Utah and California.5

U.S. census tracts

Predict: which neighborhoods will change

Models built on Census, Zillow and HUD data predicted how tracts would change (gentrify, decline, grow inclusively or stay the same) with 74% average accuracy. Rules-based methods reached 61%.6

Chicago, Illinois

Predict: which restaurant to inspect first

Chicago ranked restaurants by risk. In a two-month test in 2014, critical violations were found 7.5 days earlier, and 69% of them turned up in the first half of inspections, compared with 55%.11 A later review found that a variable for inspector group skewed the scores.12

New York, New York

Predict: fire risk for each building

FDNY’s FireCast gives about 350,000 buildings a fire-risk score. A later version was planned to use 7,500 factors from 17 agencies.13 No accuracy figures have been published.

Flint, Michigan

Decide: where to dig

A model ranked every address in Flint by how likely it was to have a lead service line. In 2017, digs guided by the model found lead at 70% of homes, rising above 80% by the end of the year. After the city stopped using the model in 2018, the rate fell to 15%.10

Here are the same examples with the type and scope of each source, which helps in judging how much weight each number can carry.

Table 8. Documented U.S. municipal GeoAI applications, by verb.

VerbExampleReported resultSource typeLimitation

Why a small team can start now

  • Most of the data is already there. Most city GIS departments already have parcels, storm drain inventories, CAD drawings, permit records and Census tables.
  • Open models are available. NASA and IBM released the Prithvi geospatial foundation model for free on Hugging Face. It’s pre-trained on satellite imagery and can be fine-tuned for jobs like flood and burn-scar mapping.7
  • Getting records into GIS can save money before any AI is involved. Carlsbad's 44% savings came from putting its records into GIS.8 That project didn't use AI, but it produced the kind of clean, mapped data a GeoAI model needs.

10. Paths for practitioners and academics

Smaller agencies and university groups can use GeoAI too. Figure 6 lays out two ways to start, one for practitioners and one for researchers. A starter toolkit for each comes after it, followed by a four-week course module.

WeekTopicActivityReading

The research notes list four open questions, including how outcomes could feed back into capital rankings and who benefits when a model decides.

11. Limits and risks

When a city acts early on a model’s predictions, it also acts early on the model’s mistakes. A few limits to keep in mind:

  • Accuracy depends on the task. The San José pilot that found potholes at 97% identified lived-in vehicles with only 12.5% accuracy.9 A single strong number says little about the whole system.
  • Data licenses limit what you can do. Imagery licenses often limit what you may extract from the pictures, even when you never train a model. Check the license before you build.
  • Predictions shape who benefits. A model that predicts which neighborhoods will rise also predicts where residents may be pushed out. Equity should be part of how the scores are calculated from the start.
  • Someone has to check the model. San José's staff verified the AI against footage. Any city using GeoAI needs someone doing the same kind of checking.

    Research Notes: Questions, Methods and Data

    How I select, verify and weigh the evidence in this series, the open questions it serves, and the GIS layer behind the maps.

    By Johan Fernandez · Updated October 1, 2026

    Central question

    How can GeoAI predict where city investments create the most value, and who benefits?

    On this page

    Research questions Review method Evidence matrix Related literature GIS layer and data dictionary Open questions

    Research questions

    1. RQ1 · Evidence. Which U.S. municipal GeoAI applications report verifiable outcomes, and how strong is that evidence? Addressed in “What Is GeoAI?” and on this page.
    2. RQ2 · Learning rankings. Can outcome feedback, as Flint's model used, improve fixed-weight Capital Improvement Plan rankings for stormwater? Upcoming stormwater case study.
    3. RQ3 · Distribution. How do equity constraints change which projects a predictive ranking funds, and who benefits? Upcoming neighborhood case study.
    4. RQ4 · Legibility. What makes a model's ranking clear enough for residents and councils to accept it? Flint example in “What Is GeoAI?”; full case study in progress.

    Review method

    This is a structured practitioner review, not a systematic review. Its rules are stated so a reader can check or repeat it.

    Scope
    U.S. city, county or state programs, 2016 to 2026.
    Include
    A deployed system, pilot or study with a published quantitative result and a source anyone can open.
    Exclude
    Vendor claims without a named deployment, and any figure that could not be traced to a source. An earlier figure of 3,600 wildfire alerts was dropped on these grounds.
    Verify
    Every figure was checked against its source page on October 1, 2026. Where a source reports another body's numbers, that is noted.

    Evidence matrix

    Every example on this site, alongside the kind of source behind it. None of the municipal examples has yet been independently peer-reviewed, which is itself a finding: deployment is outpacing evaluation. The one example that did face outside scrutiny, Chicago, was partly undercut by it.

    GIS layer and data dictionary

    The map tour runs on a point layer of the examples above, in WGS84 (EPSG:4326). It is available as GeoJSON, CSV and a zipped shapefile, with a companion state layer showing which verb each state carries. Points mark the program's home office, not every site it covers. The nationwide prediction study has no point.

    Open questions

    • Outcome data. Few cities record what happened after a capital project was built, so few rankings can learn. Which outcome measures are cheap enough to collect?
    • Independent evaluation. None of the municipal examples here has been independently peer-reviewed. Partnerships between cities and universities could close that gap.
    • Transferability. Does a model trained in one city's records hold up in another's? Flint's predictors (home age, value, location) are common, which suggests some may.
    • Fair allocation. Equal visits per district or most benefit per dollar? Flint shows the choice decides whether a model survives politically.
    Data and ethics. All data on this site is public. No personal or resident-level data is collected or shown. Corrections are welcome by email and are noted with the date.
